A 32-year-old woman comes to the physician because of fatigue and joint pain for the past 4 months. Examination shows erythema with scaling on both cheeks that spares the nasolabial folds and two 1-cm ulcers in the oral cavity. Further evaluation of this patient is most likely to show which of the following findings?

A. Decreased lymphocyte count
B. Increased platelet count
C. Increased prothrombin time
D. Decreased gamma globulin
resposta_gerada:
C

The clinical presentation of fatigue, joint pain, malar rash sparing the nasolabial folds, and oral ulcers is classic for Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE). A hallmark laboratory finding in SLE is the presence of antiphospholipid antibodies (such as lupus anticoagulant), which interfere with phospholipid-dependent coagulation tests in vitro. This interference leads to a prolonged prothrombin time (PT) and activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT), despite the patient often being at risk for thrombosis rather than bleeding. In contrast, SLE is associated with leukopenia (low white blood cell count, not specifically lymphocytes alone, though lymphopenia can occur), thrombocytopenia (low platelet count), and hypergammaglobulinemia (increased gamma globulins due to polyclonal B-cell activation). Therefore, an increased prothrombin time is the most likely finding among the choices provided.

A 66-year-old male with a history of myocardial infarction presents to your primary care office with complaints of dyspnea on exertion and swollen feet and ankles. On exam, you note an elevated JVP and 2+ pitting edema of bilateral lower extremities. What is the most likely explanation for this patient's lower extremity edema?

A. Increase in capillary pressure
B. Decrease in plasma proteins
C. Increase in capillary permeability
D. Increase in interstitial fluid pressure
resposta_gerada:
A

The patient's presentation of dyspnea on exertion, swollen feet, elevated jugular venous pressure (JVP), and a history of myocardial infarction is classic for right-sided heart failure. In heart failure, the failing right ventricle cannot effectively pump blood into the pulmonary circulation, leading to a backup of blood in the systemic venous system. This results in increased central venous pressure, which is transmitted backward to the capillaries in the lower extremities. According to Starling forces, the primary mechanism driving edema in this context is the elevation of hydrostatic pressure within the capillaries (capillary pressure), which forces fluid out of the vascular space and into the interstitial tissue. While decreased plasma proteins (hypoalbuminemia) can cause edema, it is not the primary mechanism in heart failure, and increased capillary permeability is more characteristic of inflammatory states like cellulitis or burns. Increased interstitial fluid pressure is a consequence of the edema rather than the initial cause.

A 49-year-old man comes to the physician because he has had multiple falls and multiple episodes of dizziness over the past 6 weeks. There is no personal or family history of serious illness. He drinks one pint of rum daily. He works as a foreman in a factory that produces industrial solvents. He is alert and oriented to time, place, and person. His temperature is 36.7°C (98.1°F), pulse is 88/min, and blood pressure is 108/70 mm Hg. Examination shows a wide-based gait. The patient is unable to stand with his feet together without support. There is a coarse tremor of the hands when he is asked to grab a pen. Muscle strength and tone are normal in all extremities. Sensation to pain, vibration, and position is intact bilaterally. Rapid alternating movements of the hands is impaired. Mental status examination shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's condition?

A. Korsakoff syndrome
B. Methanol poisoning
C. Cerebellar degeneration
D. Wernicke's encephalopathy
resposta_gerada:
C

The patient presents with classic signs of cerebellar dysfunction, including a wide-based gait, inability to tandem walk (Romberg sign positive), coarse tremor, and dysdiadochokinesia (impaired rapid alternating movements). The key to identifying the cause lies in his history of chronic heavy alcohol consumption ("one pint of rum daily"). Chronic alcohol use is a leading cause of toxic-metabolic cerebellar degeneration, which typically affects the anterior vermis of the cerebellum. This condition manifests primarily as gait ataxia and truncal instability, often with preserved limb coordination until later stages, though fine motor tasks like writing can also be affected.

While the patient has a history of alcohol use, the absence of confusion, ophthalmoplegia, or nystagmus makes acute Wernicke's encephalopathy (Option D) unlikely. Korsakoff syndrome (Option A) is characterized by anterograde amnesia and confabulation, which are not present here. Methanol poisoning (Option B) typically presents with visual disturbances (blindness) and metabolic acidosis, neither of which are described. Therefore, chronic alcohol-induced cerebellar degeneration is the most likely diagnosis.

The first 24 hours after delivery, a 2888 g (6.37 lb) male newborn is not feeding well, has a high-pitched cry, and is diaphoretic. He was born at 38 weeks' gestation to a 30-year-old woman, gravida 2, para 1, after an uncomplicated labor and delivery. Apgar scores were 8 and 9 at 1 and 5 minutes, respectively. The mother did not receive prenatal care. She takes codeine syrup frequently for dry cough. The infant's temperature is 37.8°C (100°F), pulse is 165/min, and blood pressure is 83/50 mm Hg. Examination shows hyperreflexia, tremors, and an excessive startle response. The baby is swaddled to prevent excoriations, and fluid resuscitation is initiated. Complete blood count and serum levels of glucose, bilirubin, and calcium are within normal limits. What is the most appropriate next step in treatment of this newborn?

A. Oral morphine therapy
B. Intravenous ampicillin and gentamicin combination therapy
C. Oral methimazole therapy
D. Dextrose infusion
resposta_gerada:
D

The clinical presentation of a newborn with poor feeding, high-pitched cry, diaphoresis, hyperreflexia, tremors, and an excessive startle response (hypertonia) is classic for **neonatal abstinence syndrome (NAS)**, also known as neonatal withdrawal. The mother's history of frequent codeine syrup use is the likely etiology, as opioids cross the placenta and the infant experiences withdrawal after birth when the drug supply is cut off.

The initial management for NAS involves supportive care, which includes a quiet environment, swaddling, and adequate nutrition and hydration. The vignette states that the infant is already swaddled and receiving fluid resuscitation. However, the infant remains symptomatic (not feeding well, diaphoretic, tremors). When supportive measures are insufficient to control symptoms, the standard of care is to initiate pharmacologic treatment. **Morphine** (or sometimes methadone) is the first-line medication for treating moderate to severe opioid withdrawal in newborns.

Let's evaluate the other options:
*   **B. Intravenous ampicillin and gentamicin:** This is the empiric treatment for early-onset sepsis. While sepsis can present with similar symptoms (poor feeding, temperature instability), the infant's CBC, glucose, bilirubin, and calcium are normal, and the specific constellation of hyperreflexia and tremors strongly points to withdrawal rather than infection. Furthermore, the mother's history of codeine use provides a clear alternative diagnosis.
*   **C. Oral methimazole therapy:** This is used to treat hyperthyroidism (e.g., Graves' disease). While maternal hyperthyroidism can cause a hyperactive infant, the specific history of opioid use and the classic withdrawal signs make this incorrect.
*   **D. Dextrose infusion:** The vignette explicitly states that serum glucose levels are within normal limits, so treating for hypoglycemia is unnecessary.

Therefore, since supportive care is ongoing but symptoms persist, the most appropriate next step is to start opioid replacement therapy with morphine.

Answer: A

According to USPSTF guidelines, screening for osteoporosis with dual-energy x-ray absorptiometry (DXA) is recommended for all women aged 65 years and older, but it is also indicated for postmenopausal women younger than 65 who have risk factors for osteoporosis or a prior fragility fracture. Given her low BMI, smoking history, and heavy alcohol use, she meets the criteria for screening. The other options are not indicated: her Pap smear and colonoscopy were normal within the recommended intervals, abdominal ultrasound is not a routine screening tool for her conditions, and while the S4 gallop suggests left ventricular hypertrophy (likely due to hypertension), a transesophageal echocardiogram is an invasive diagnostic test not appropriate for routine screening or initial evaluation of an asymptomatic patient.

There has been a grape-like mass protruding from her vagina for the last 15 days. On examination, the fundus of the uterus is at the level of the umbilicus and no fetal heart sounds are heard. resposta_gerada:
C

The patient's presentation of fatigue, shortness of breath, ankle swelling, and a widely split S2 that varies with respiration (fixed splitting is typical of ASD, but a widely split S2 that varies suggests right ventricular volume overload or delayed closure of the pulmonary valve) combined with an ECG showing right bundle branch block (RBBB) strongly indicates right-sided heart failure. In right heart failure, the right ventricle fails to pump blood effectively into the pulmonary circulation, leading to a backup of blood in the systemic venous system. This results in elevated central venous pressure, which is transmitted back to the lower extremity veins. The increased pressure within the venous system is transmitted to the capillaries, raising the capillary hydrostatic pressure. According to Starling forces, this increased hydrostatic pressure forces fluid out of the capillaries and into the interstitial space, causing pitting edema. While sleep apnea can contribute to pulmonary hypertension and subsequent right heart failure, the direct mechanism for the edema is the hemodynamic consequence of the heart failure. Options A and B would typically present with unilateral or asymmetric findings, and Option D (decreased oncotic pressure) is more commonly associated with liver failure or nephrotic syndrome, which do not fit the specific cardiac findings described here.

A 46-year-old woman comes to the physician because of severe muscle and joint pain for 5 months. The pain varies in location and intensity. She also has joint stiffness in the morning and reports fatigue throughout the day that she attributes to not sleeping well. She reports a tingling sensation in her lower limbs. Her bowel habits are unchanged but she often feels bloated. She has primary hypertension and occasional migraine headaches. She does not smoke or consume alcohol. Her medications include propranolol and sumatriptan. She appears healthy. Examination shows symmetric muscular tenderness at the base of the neck, over the shoulders, and in the lumbosacral area. Strength and deep tendon reflexes are normal. Laboratory studies show:
Hemoglobin 14.3 g/dL
Leukocyte count 9300/mm3
Platelet count 230,000/mm3
Mean corpuscular volume 85 μm3
Erythrocyte sedimentation rate 12 mm/h
Serum
Glucose 92 mg/dL
Creatinine 0.6 mg/dL
TSH 3.1 μU/mL
Urinalysis is within normal limits. Which of the following is the most appropriate therapy for this patient?"

A. Temazepam
B. Vitamin B12
C. Amitriptyline
D. Methotrexate
"
resposta_gerada:
C

The patient's presentation of widespread, fluctuating muscle and joint pain, morning stiffness, fatigue, and paresthesias, combined with a normal physical examination (normal strength and reflexes) and normal inflammatory markers (ESR 12 mm/h), is classic for **fibromyalgia**. The tingling sensation and bloating may be related to comorbid small fiber neuropathy or irritable bowel syndrome, which frequently coexist with fibromyalgia. Since there is no evidence of inflammatory arthritis (normal ESR, symmetric tenderness without swelling) or vitamin deficiency (normal MCV, no specific risk factors mentioned for B12 deficiency), the most appropriate first-line pharmacologic therapy is a low-dose tricyclic antidepressant, such as **amitriptyline**, which helps improve sleep and reduce pain perception. Temazepam is a benzodiazepine not indicated for chronic pain management due to addiction risk. Vitamin B12 is unnecessary given normal labs, and methotrexate is used for inflammatory conditions like rheumatoid arthritis, which this patient does not have.

A 35-year-old woman comes to the physician because of intermittent episodes of heart palpitations for 3 weeks. The palpitations are accompanied by chest pain that is sharp and localized to the left 3rd intercostal space. The patient does not smoke. She drinks one to two glasses of wine on the weekends. She appears nervous. Her pulse is 110/min and irregularly irregular, and blood pressure is 135/85 mmHg. Examination shows a fine tremor on both hands and digital swelling. There is retraction of the left upper eyelid. A systolic ejection murmur is heard along the right upper sternal border. The extremities are warm, and pulses are 2+ bilaterally. Which of the following is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy?

A. Propranolol
B. Digoxin
C. Amiodarone
D. Warfarin
resposta_gerada:
A

The patient's presentation of an irregularly irregular pulse, fine tremor, digital swelling (pretibial myxedema), and lid retraction (thyroid dermopathy) is classic for Graves' disease with thyrotoxicosis. The palpitations and chest pain are likely due to the high sympathetic tone and atrial fibrillation associated with the hyperthyroid state.

In patients with thyrotoxicosis who develop atrial fibrillation, the primary goal of pharmacotherapy is to control the heart rate and manage the adrenergic symptoms. Beta-blockers, such as **Propranolol**, are the first-line treatment in this scenario. They effectively reduce heart rate, alleviate palpitations, and treat the underlying adrenergic excess caused by excess thyroid hormone. Additionally, Propranolol has a unique property among beta-blockers: it can inhibit the peripheral conversion of T4 to the more active T3, providing a dual benefit in treating the underlying hyperthyroidism while managing cardiac symptoms.

Digoxin is generally ineffective for rate control in thyrotoxic atrial fibrillation because the increased sensitivity of the heart to catecholamines in hyperthyroid states often renders digoxin less effective. Amiodarone is typically reserved for cases where beta-blockers are contraindicated or ineffective, though it carries a risk of inducing or worsening thyroid dysfunction (amiodarone-induced thyrotoxicosis). Warfarin is an anticoagulant used to prevent thromboembolism in atrial fibrillation but does not address the immediate symptoms of tachycardia or the underlying thyrotoxicosis; furthermore, the decision to anticoagulate depends on the CHA₂DS₂-VASc score, which is not the primary focus of the acute symptom management described here.

A 5-year-old boy is brought to his pediatrician due to sore throat and fever. He was in his usual state of health until 3 days ago when he began to complain of a sore throat as well as general malaise. The patient's past medical history reveals recurrent upper respiratory infections but no skin or soft tissue infections. The child had cardiac surgery as an infant but has otherwise been healthy. On presentation, his temperature is 100°F (37.8 °C), blood pressure is 115/72 mmHg, pulse is 65/min, and respirations are 22/min. Physical exam shows white plaques on the tongue and mouth. A scraping of this material reveals a characteristic morphology after being treated with KOH. Serum protein electrophoresis shows a normal distribution of bands from this patient. Which of the following findings would most likely be found in this patient?

A. Delayed separation of the umbilical cord
B. Hypoparathyroidism
C. Partial albinism
D. Thrombocytopenic purpura
resposta_gerada:
C

The clinical presentation of white plaques on the tongue and mouth that are removed by scraping (pseudomembranes) is characteristic of **Candidiasis** (oral thrush). In a 5-year-old child, the presence of thrush is often a sign of an underlying immunodeficiency or hematologic disorder, as healthy children typically clear fungal infections easily. The key to identifying the specific condition lies in the combination of symptoms: recurrent infections, oral candidiasis, and the specific mention of **partial albinism** as a potential finding.

This triad (recurrent infections, candidiasis, and albinism) is classic for **Chediak-Higashi syndrome**, an autosomal recessive disorder caused by a mutation in the *LYST* gene. This defect leads to impaired microtubule polymerization in lysosomes, resulting in giant granules in leukocytes (which causes the recurrent infections and failure to clear Candida) and defective melanosome transport (which causes partial albinism). The normal serum protein electrophoresis helps rule out conditions like Multiple Myeloma or significant paraproteinemia, though it is less specific for this pediatric case.

Let's evaluate the other options:
*   **A. Delayed separation of the umbilical cord:** This is a hallmark of **Leukocyte Adhesion Deficiency (LAD)**. While LAD presents with recurrent bacterial infections and delayed cord separation, it does not typically present with oral candidiasis or albinism.
*   **B. Hypoparathyroidism:** This is associated with DiGeorge syndrome (22q11.2 deletion). DiGeorge syndrome presents with hypocalcemia, thymic aplasia (leading to T-cell deficiency), and cardiac defects. While it can cause infections, the specific combination of thrush and albinism points more strongly to Chediak-Higashi. Furthermore, the cardiac surgery history in the vignette could be a distractor or a red herring, but the specific "white plaques" + "albinism" link is the strongest diagnostic clue.
*   **D. Thrombocytopenic purpura:** This refers to Immune Thrombocytopenia (ITP), which presents with low platelets and bleeding, not primarily with fungal infections or albinism.

Therefore, the finding most likely associated with this patient's underlying condition (Chediak-Higashi syndrome) is partial albinism.

A 21-month-old boy is brought to the physician for a well-child examination. His mother noticed deformities in both of his legs since he started walking independently. He has been healthy apart from an upper respiratory tract infection 6 months ago. He was delivered at 38 weeks' gestation. His 6-year-old sister was treated for developmental dysplasia of the hip. He can kick a ball and say a 2-word phrase. He plays well with other children at his day care. His immunizations are up-to-date. He is at the 40th percentile for height and 50th percentile for weight. Vital signs are within normal limits. Examination shows closed anterior and posterior fontanelles. The knees do not stay together when both the feet and ankles are placed together. The gait is unremarkable. The mother is concerned that he has a growth disorder. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

A. Vitamin D supplementation
B. Reassurance and follow-up
C. X-ray of the lower extremities
D. Bracing of the lower extremities
resposta_gerada:
B. Reassurance and follow-up

The clinical presentation is consistent with physiologic genu varum (bow-leggedness), which is a normal finding in toddlers. This condition is most prominent between 12 and 24 months of age as children begin to walk and typically resolves spontaneously by age 3 to 4 years as the tibia undergoes physiologic bowing and then straightening. The child's normal growth parameters, healthy history, and lack of pain or gait disturbance further support a benign, self-limiting condition. Immediate imaging (X-ray) or interventions like bracing or vitamin D supplementation are not indicated unless there are signs of pathology such as persistent deformity beyond age 3, asymmetric bowing, pain, or failure to thrive.

A 44-year-old woman presents to her primary care physician because she has been having fever, chest pain, and cough for the last several weeks. She presented to the physician because she discovered blood in her sputum after coughing. She recently returned from a year of traveling abroad, but has otherwise been healthy. Based on clinical suspicion, an acid fast stain is performed showing the causative organism, and she is started on appropriate therapy. Two weeks later, she returns with a skin rash, diarrhea, and confusion, and is given a factor to take in addition to the medications previously prescribed. Which of the following is a characteristic of the factor that was most likely provided?

A. Required for collagen hydroxylation
B. Required for dehydrogenase enzymes
C. Required for methionine processing
D. Required for methylmalonyl-CoA processing
resposta_gerada:
D

The patient's presentation of chronic cough, fever, chest pain, hemoptysis, and travel history is classic for pulmonary tuberculosis (TB), confirmed by the acid-fast stain. The subsequent development of a skin rash, diarrhea, and confusion two weeks after starting appropriate therapy (likely rifampin, isoniazid, and pyrazinamide) indicates **Isoniazid (INH) toxicity**, specifically peripheral neuropathy or encephalopathy, which is a known side effect of INH.

Isoniazid works by inhibiting mycolic acid synthesis in mycobacteria, but in humans, it interferes with the metabolism of Vitamin B6 (pyridoxine). INH forms a hydrazide complex with pyridoxal phosphate (the active form of B6), depleting its levels. Pyridoxal phosphate is an essential cofactor for several enzymes, most notably **pyridoxal phosphokinase** and enzymes involved in amino acid metabolism. Crucially, Vitamin B6 is required as a cofactor for **methionine synthase** (which converts homocysteine to methionine) and is involved in the processing of methionine and other amino acids. The confusion and rash can be signs of B6 deficiency or hypersensitivity, and the "factor" provided is likely pyridoxine (Vitamin B6).

Let's evaluate the options based on Vitamin B6 (pyridoxine) function:
*   **A. Required for collagen hydroxylation:** This requires Vitamin C (ascorbic acid).
*   **B. Required for dehydrogenase enzymes:** While B6 is involved in transamination, the specific "dehydrogenase" requirement is most famously associated with NAD+/NADP+ or FAD/FMN (Vitamins B3 and B2).
*   **C. Required for methionine processing:** Vitamin B6 (as pyridoxal phosphate) is a cofactor for enzymes involved in methionine metabolism, including the conversion of homocysteine to methionine via methionine synthase (though B12 is the direct cofactor for the synthase, B6 is required for the regeneration of the methyl donor or related transsulfuration pathways involving cystathionine beta-synthase). More broadly, B6 is central to amino acid processing, including methionine.
*   **D. Required for methylmalonyl-CoA processing:** This requires Vitamin B12 (cobalamin) as a cofactor for methylmalonyl-CoA mutase.

Wait, let's re-evaluate the specific metabolic pathway often tested with B6. B6 is the cofactor for **cystathionine beta-synthase** (homocysteine to cystathionine) and **serine hydroxymethyltransferase**. The conversion of homocysteine to methionine requires B12 and Folate. However, the question asks about the factor provided. If the patient has INH toxicity, they are given Pyridoxine. What is a characteristic of Pyridoxine?
Pyridoxine is a cofactor for:
1.  Transamination (Aminotransferases)
2.  Decarboxylation (Aromatic L-amino acid decarboxylase, etc.)
3.  Glycosylation
4.  **Methionine processing**? Actually, the transsulfuration pathway (Homocysteine -> Cystathionine -> Cysteine) is the major B6-dependent pathway for methionine *catabolism*. The remethylation of homocysteine to methionine requires B12.
Let's look at Option C again: "Required for methionine processing". This is a bit ambiguous.
Let's look at Option D again: "Required for methylmalonyl-CoA processing". This is definitely B12.
Let's look at Option A: Vitamin C.
Let's look at Option B: "Required for dehydrogenase enzymes". This is vague.

Is it possible the question implies the patient was given **Vitamin B12**? No, INH toxicity is treated with B6.
Perhaps the "factor" is something else? The symptoms (rash, diarrhea, confusion) could be **Pyrazinamide** toxicity (hyperuricemia, hepatotoxicity) or **Rifampin** (orange fluids, CYP induction). But the classic board association with TB meds and a new neurological/dermatological issue is INH -> B6 deficiency.
If the answer is B6, which option fits best?
B6 is a cofactor for **cystathionine beta-synthase**. This enzyme processes methionine (by converting homocysteine, a derivative of methionine, into cystathionine). Therefore, B6 is required for the processing of methionine derivatives.
However, sometimes questions conflate the pathways. Let's reconsider the "factor". Could it be **Vitamin B12** given for something else? No, the clinical vignette screams INH toxicity.
Let's re-read the options carefully.
A: Vit C.
B: Dehydrogenases (NAD/FAD).
C: Methionine processing.
D: Methylmalonyl-CoA processing (B12).

If the answer is B6, C is the closest fit because B6 is essential for the transsulfuration pathway of methionine. Without B6, homocysteine accumulates (though not via the B12-dependent step).
Is there any other interpretation?
Maybe the "factor" is **Vitamin B12** and the diagnosis is something else? No, acid-fast stain = TB. TB tx = RIPE.
INH causes B6 deficiency. Treatment = Pyridoxine.
Pyridoxine (B6) functions:
- Transamination
- Decarboxylation
- **Cystathionine synthase** (Methionine -> Homocysteine -> Cystathionine). This is "methionine processing".
- Glycosylation.

Therefore, Option C is the correct characteristic of Vitamin B6 among the choices provided. Option D is strictly B12. Option A is strictly Vit C. Option B is generally NAD/FAD.

**Correct Answer:** C
**Justification:** The patient is suffering from Isoniazid (INH) toxicity, a common side effect of TB treatment, which depletes Vitamin B6 (pyridoxine) stores. The "factor" provided is pyridoxine. Vitamin B6 is a cofactor for cystathionine beta-synthase, an enzyme in the transsulfuration pathway that processes methionine (converting homocysteine to cystathionine). Thus, it is required for methionine processing. Option D describes the function of Vitamin B12.

A 64-year-old man with coronary artery disease and hypertension comes to the physician for a follow-up examination. His blood pressure ranged from 160/100 mm Hg to 150/94 mm Hg on his previous 3 visits over the past 4 months. Current medications include aspirin, atorvastatin, hydrochlorothiazide, and metoprolol. Three weeks ago, he was also started on amlodipine. His blood pressure today is 158/98 mm Hg. Physical examination shows no other abnormalities. Renal duplex ultrasonography shows 90% occlusion of the right renal artery. Decreased renal blood flow is most likely to cause which of the following?

A. Hyperplasia of juxtaglomerular cells
B. Dilation of efferent arteriole
C. Decreased prostaglandin synthesis by macula densa
D. Decreased reabsorption of bicarbonate at proximal tubule
resposta_gerada:
A. Hyperplasia of juxtaglomerular cells

**Justification:**
The patient has significant renal artery stenosis (90% occlusion), which leads to decreased perfusion pressure in the afferent arteriole of the affected kidney. In response to this hypoperfusion, the juxtaglomerular apparatus detects the drop in pressure and releases renin. This triggers the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS). Chronic stimulation of the juxtaglomerular cells by low perfusion pressure and sympathetic tone leads to their hypertrophy and hyperplasia. Additionally, angiotensin II causes preferential constriction of the efferent arteriole (not dilation) to maintain glomerular filtration pressure, and the macula densa typically responds to low flow by increasing prostaglandin synthesis to dilate the afferent arteriole, not decreasing it. While RAAS activation increases sodium and water reabsorption, the primary structural adaptation to the chronic hypoperfusion described is the cellular proliferation of the juxtaglomerular cells.

A 35-year-old woman comes to the physician for genetic counseling prior to conception. Her younger brother has mild developmental delay, pale complexion, and has to limit his dietary intake of phenylalanine. She has no similar symptoms and is in good health. Her parents are healthy. Which of the following is the most appropriate assessment of her carrier status for the disease affecting her brother?

A. 67%
B. 100%
C. 75%
D. 50%
resposta_gerada:
D

The clinical presentation of the patient's brother (developmental delay, pale complexion, and dietary restriction of phenylalanine) is classic for Phenylketonuria (PKU), an autosomal recessive disorder. In autosomal recessive inheritance, affected individuals are homozygous recessive (aa). Since the parents are healthy, they must both be heterozygous carriers (Aa). For each pregnancy, the possible genotypes are AA (25%), Aa (50%), and aa (25%). The patient is unaffected, which means she is not the aa genotype. Therefore, we condition our probability on the fact that she is either AA or Aa. Among the unaffected offspring of two carrier parents, the ratio of AA to Aa is 1:2. Consequently, the probability that she is a carrier (Aa) is 2 out of 3, or approximately 67%. However, looking at the provided options, 67% is Option A. Wait, let me re-evaluate the standard calculation versus the options provided.

Standard calculation:
Parents: Aa x Aa
Offspring probabilities: 1/4 AA, 1/2 Aa, 1/4 aa.
Given the patient is unaffected (not aa), the sample space is reduced to the 3/4 chance of being unaffected.
Probability of being a carrier (Aa) given unaffected = (1/2) / (3/4) = 2/3 ≈ 66.7%.

Let's re-read the options.
A. 67%
B. 100%
C. 75%
D. 50%

The calculated value is ~67%. This matches Option A.

Wait, did I misread the question or the options? Let me double check common pitfalls. Sometimes questions ask for the probability of the *brother* being a carrier (which would be 2/3 if he were unaffected, but he is affected). No, the question asks about *her* carrier status.

Is there any scenario where the answer is 50%?
If the disease were X-linked recessive:
Brother is affected (XaY). Mother is a carrier (XAXa). Father is normal (XAY).
Daughter receives XA from father. She receives either XA or Xa from mother.
Probability she is a carrier (XAXa) is 50%.
Does PKU fit X-linked? No, PKU is autosomal recessive. The symptoms (developmental delay, phenylalanine restriction) are definitive for PKU.

Let's reconsider the calculation for Autosomal Recessive.
Parents: Carrier x Carrier.
Child possibilities: 25% Normal (AA), 50% Carrier (Aa), 25% Affected (aa).
We know the woman is NOT affected. So we exclude the 25% aa group.
Remaining pool: 25% AA + 50% Aa = 75% total unaffected.
Probability she is a carrier = (50%) / (75%) = 2/3 = 66.66...%
This rounds to 67%.

So Option A (67%) is the mathematically correct answer for an autosomal recessive condition.

However, let me look at Option D (50%). Is it possible the question implies a different inheritance pattern or I am missing a nuance?
If the question implies the parents are not known carriers but the brother is affected, the parents *must* be carriers.
Is it possible the question is a trick and the answer is actually 50%? No, the Bayesian update for unaffected siblings of an affected individual in AR diseases is universally taught as 2/3.

Let's check if there is any ambiguity about "pale complexion". PKU patients can have hypopigmentation (fair skin/hair) due to lack of melanin synthesis from phenylalanine/tyrosine pathway. This confirms AR.

Therefore, the calculation stands: 2/3 = 67%.
Option A is 67%.

Wait, I need to be careful. Sometimes in multiple choice questions, if 2/3 isn't an option, they might simplify or I might be misinterpreting the "healthy" status. But 67% is explicitly an option.

Let's re-verify the options list provided in the prompt.
A. 67%
B. 100%
C. 75%
D. 50%

The correct answer is A.

**Correction/Refinement**:
Wait, I see a potential issue. In some simplified contexts or specific exam boards, they might erroneously select 50% if they forget to condition on the unaffected status, but that would be incorrect medical genetics. Or, perhaps the question is designed to test the 2/3 rule specifically.
Let's assume the standard rigorous medical genetics approach.
1. Disease: Phenylketonuria (Autosomal Recessive).
2. Parents: Both obligate carriers (Aa).
3. Patient: Unaffected female.
4. Possible genotypes for patient: AA (1/3 of unaffected), Aa (2/3 of unaffected).
5. Probability of being a carrier: 2/3 = 66.7%.

This aligns perfectly with Option A.

**Final check**:
Could it be X-linked? No, PKU is not X-linked.
Could it be mitochondrial? No.
So, Autosomal Recessive.
Probability = 2/3.
2/3 is approximately 67%.

Therefore, the correct option is A.

Answer: A

A 29-year-old man is brought to the emergency department by a concerned neighbor. The patient appears disheveled, has a flat affect, and appears to be having auditory hallucinations. He is alert and oriented to time, person, and place and has an intact long-term and short-term memory. His neighbor says that he never really knew the patient that well and that he mostly kept to himself. They have been neighbors for the past 3 years at an apartment close to the hospital. What worried the neighbor was a sudden change in the patient's behavior which started last week. He suddenly seemed interested in attending all the local council meetings and social gatherings. He is very talkative at these events and boasts highly of himself and starts suggesting changes that the committee could make with his help. He gets very agitated when they deny accepting his suggestions. Which of the following is a predictor of good prognosis for this patient's condition?

A. Affective symptoms
B. Being single
C. Male sex
D. Negative symptoms
resposta_gerada:
D

The clinical presentation of a sudden onset of grandiosity, decreased need for sleep (implied by high energy/socializing), and agitation in a previously withdrawn individual is highly suggestive of a manic episode, likely secondary to a primary psychotic disorder like schizophrenia or a primary mood disorder with psychotic features. When evaluating prognostic factors for schizophrenia (the most common context for such questions regarding negative vs. positive symptoms), the presence of **negative symptoms** (such as flat affect, avolition, and social withdrawal) at onset is a strong predictor of a poorer prognosis. Conversely, the **absence** of negative symptoms, the presence of **affective symptoms** (mood symptoms like mania or depression), and a later age of onset are predictors of a **better prognosis**. Since the patient currently exhibits prominent positive symptoms (hallucinations, grandiosity) and affective symptoms (agitation, mania) without mentioned negative symptoms, the presence of affective symptoms and the lack of negative symptoms point toward a more favorable outcome compared to cases dominated by negative symptoms. Among the choices provided, "Affective symptoms" is the recognized positive prognostic indicator. Being single, male sex, and the presence of negative symptoms are all associated with a worse prognosis.

pergunta:
Background:
Some patients with severe asthma have frequent exacerbations associated with persistent eosinophilic inflammation despite continuous treatment with high-dose inhaled glucocorticoids with or without oral glucocorticoids.
Methods:
In this randomized, double-blind clinical trial we assigned 576 patients with recurrent asthma exacerbations and evidence of eosinophilic inflammation despite high doses of inhaled glucocorticoids to one of three study groups. Patients were assigned to receive mepolizumab, a humanized monoclonal antibody against interleukin-5, which was administered as either a 75-mg intravenous dose or a 100-mg subcutaneous dose or placebo every 4 weeks for 32 weeks. The primary outcome was the rate of exacerbations. Other outcomes included the forced expiratory volume in 1 second (FEV1) and scores on the St. George’s Respiratory Questionnaire (SGRQ) and the 5-item Asthma Control Questionnaire (ACQ-5).
Results:
The rate of exacerbations was reduced by 47% (95% confidence interval [CI], 29 to 61) among patients receiving intravenous mepolizumab and by 53% (95% CI, 37 to 65) among those receiving subcutaneous mepolizumab, as compared with those receiving placebo (p<0.001 for both comparisons). Exacerbations necessitating an emergency department visit or hospitalization were reduced by 32% in the group receiving intravenous mepolizumab and by 61% in the group receiving subcutaneous mepolizumab. At week 32, the mean increase from baseline in FEV1 was 100 ml greater in patients receiving intravenous mepolizumab than in those receiving placebo (p=0.02) and 98 ml greater in patients receiving subcutaneous mepolizumab than in those receiving placebo (p=0.03). The improvement from baseline in the SGRQ score was 6.4 points and 7.0 points greater in the intravenous and subcutaneous mepolizumab groups, respectively than in the placebo group, and the improvement in the ACQ-5 score was 0.42 points and 0.44 points greater in the two mepolizumab groups, respectively than in the placebo group (p<0.001 for all comparisons).
Conclusions:
Mepolizumab administered either intravenously or subcutaneously significantly reduced asthma exacerbations and was associated with improvements in markers of asthma control.
Given the original research abstract above, which of the following would be true if the authors had inadvertently encountered a type 1 error?

A. A type 1 error occurs when the null hypothesis is true but is rejected in error.
B. A type 1 error occurs when the null hypothesis is false, yet is accepted in error.
C. A type 1 error is a beta (β) error and is usually 0.1 or 0.2.
D. A type 1 error is dependent on the confidence interval of a study.
resposta_gerada:
A. A type 1 error occurs when the null hypothesis is true but is rejected in error.

**Justification:** In statistical hypothesis testing, a Type 1 error (false positive) happens when the null hypothesis ($H_0$) is actually true (meaning there is no real difference between the treatment and placebo), but the study results lead to the incorrect rejection of $H_0$ in favor of the alternative hypothesis. Option B describes a Type 2 error (false negative). Option C is incorrect because a Type 1 error is denoted by alpha ($\alpha$), not beta ($\beta$), and beta corresponds to the probability of a Type 2 error. Option D is incorrect because the Type 1 error rate is determined by the significance level ($\alpha$) set by the researchers (commonly 0.05), not directly by the calculated confidence interval of the specific study results, although the CI relates to the significance level.
resposta_esperada: A type 1 error occurs when the null hypothesis is true but is rejected in error.

pergunta:
A 21-year-old female presents to the clinic requesting prenatal counseling. She was born with a disease that has led her to have recurrent upper respiratory infections throughout her life requiring antibiotic prophylaxis and chest physiotherapy as well as pancreatic enzyme replacement therapy. She marries a man (without this disease phenotype) from a population where the prevalence of this disease is 1/100. What is the chance that their child will have the disease of interest?

A. 9/100
B. 1/10
C. 81/100
D. 9/10
resposta_gerada:
D

The clinical presentation of recurrent respiratory infections requiring chest physiotherapy and pancreatic enzyme replacement therapy is classic for Cystic Fibrosis (CF), an autosomal recessive disorder. The question states the prevalence of the disease in the population is 1/100. In Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium terms, $q^2 = 1/100$, which means the frequency of the disease allele ($q$) is $1/10$. Consequently, the frequency of the normal allele ($p$) is $9/10$.

The woman is affected, so she is homozygous recessive ($aa$) and will definitely pass one recessive allele to her child. The man is unaffected, but since he is from the same population, we must calculate the probability that he is a carrier ($Aa$). The frequency of carriers in the population is $2pq = 2 \times (9/10) \times (1/10) = 18/100$. However, we know he is not affected, so we must condition on him being in the unaffected population ($p^2 + 2pq$). The probability he is a carrier given he is unaffected is $(2pq) / (p^2 + 2pq) = (18/100) / (81/100 + 18/100) = 18/99 = 2/11$.

Wait, let's re-evaluate the standard interpretation for this specific type of board question. Often, if the question implies the man is a random individual from the population *who happens to be unaffected*, the calculation is as above. However, let's look at the answer choices. They are simple fractions like 9/100, 1/10, 81/100, 9/10.

Let's reconsider the allele frequency calculation. If $q^2 = 1/100$, then $q = 0.1$ and $p = 0.9$.
The probability the man is a carrier is $2pq / (1 - q^2) = 2(0.9)(0.1) / (0.99) = 0.18 / 0.99 = 2/11$.
If the man is a carrier, the chance of the child getting the disease (receiving 'a' from mom and 'a' from dad) is $1/2 \times 1/2 = 1/4$.
Total probability = $(2/11) \times (1/4) = 2/44 = 1/22$. This is not an option.

Is it possible the question assumes the "prevalence" refers to the carrier frequency? No, it says "prevalence of this disease".
Is it possible the question simplifies the math by ignoring the denominator correction for the unaffected male?
If we assume the probability the man is a carrier is simply $2q$ (approximation where $p \approx 1$) or just use $2pq$ directly without dividing by $1-q^2$?

An asymptomatic 65-year-old woman is found to have T-score of -2.6 SD on routine bone mineral density screening. She has a 10-year history of hypertension and an esophageal stricture due to severe gastroesophageal reflux disease. She was diagnosed with endometrial hyperplasia 20 years ago and treated with medroxyprogesterone. Menarche started at 11 years of age and her last menstrual period was 8 years ago. Her last mammography and PAP smear 6 months ago showed no abnormalities. Her mother died of breast cancer at the age of 45 years. The patient does not have any children. Current medications include lansoprazole and hydrochlorothiazide. Her blood pressure is 135/85 mm Hg. Physical examination shows no abnormalities. Treatment is begun with a drug that prevents further bone resorption and reduces her risk of developing breast cancer. This drug puts her at an increased risk of which of the following adverse effects?

A. Skin infections
B. Osteosarcoma
C. Hypercholesterolemia
D. Deep vein thrombosis
"
resposta_gerada:
D

The patient has osteoporosis (T-score ≤ -2.5) and a significant family history of breast cancer (mother died at 45). The treatment described is **raloxifene**, a selective estrogen receptor modulator (SERM). Raloxifene acts as an estrogen agonist in bone (preventing resorption) and an antagonist in breast tissue (reducing the risk of invasive breast cancer). However, like tamoxifen, raloxifene increases the risk of **venous thromboembolism**, including deep vein thrombosis (DVT) and pulmonary embolism. It is also associated with an increased risk of hot flashes and cataracts, but not skin infections, osteosarcoma, or hypercholesterolemia (it may actually lower LDL cholesterol).

A 25-year-old woman comes to the physician because of irregular menstrual bleeding. Menses have occurred at 30- to 90-day intervals since menarche at the age of 12 years. Her last menstrual period was 6 weeks ago. She is sexually active with her husband and they do not use condoms. There is no personal or family history of serious illness. She is 170 cm (5 ft 7 in) tall and weighs 73 kg (161 lb); BMI is 25.3 kg/m2. Her vital signs are within normal limits. Examination shows oily skin and severe acne on the face. There is dark hair on the upper lip and around both nipples. Laboratory studies show:
Dehydroepiandrosterone sulfate 6.2 μg/mL (N=0.5–5.4)
Follicle-stimulating hormone 20 mIU/mL
Luteinizing hormone 160 mIU/mL
Testosterone 4.1 nmol/L (N < 3.5)
A urine pregnancy test is negative. Which of the following tests is the most appropriate next step in screening for comorbidities in this patient?"

A. 17-hydroxyprogesterone and cortisol level measurements
B. CA-125 level measurement
C. Blood glucose and cholesterol level measurements
D. TSH and T4 level measurements
resposta_gerada:
C

This patient presents with signs of hyperandrogenism (severe acne, hirsutism, irregular menses) and an elevated LH:FSH ratio, which is highly suggestive of Polycystic Ovary Syndrome (PCOS). According to clinical guidelines (such as those from the Endocrine Society and ACOG), once PCOS is diagnosed, it is essential to screen for associated metabolic comorbidities due to the high prevalence of insulin resistance and dyslipidemia in this population. Therefore, measuring fasting blood glucose (or HbA1c) and a lipid profile (cholesterol) is the most appropriate next step. While 17-hydroxyprogesterone is used to rule out non-classic congenital adrenal hyperplasia (a differential diagnosis), the question specifically asks for screening for *comorbidities* of the likely diagnosis, making metabolic screening the priority. CA-125 is not indicated for PCOS screening, and while TSH should be checked to rule out thyroid dysfunction as a cause of oligomenorrhea, the metabolic risks associated with PCOS are a more direct and critical comorbidity to address in this context.
resposta_esperada: Blood glucose and cholesterol level measurements

A 7 -day-old newborn boy presents to the emergency department with a history of fever, irritability, and generalized erythema. During the first 2 days of clinical manifestations, the parents of the child tried to control the symptoms using acetaminophen; however, the newborn continued to be ill, and blisters were noticeable around the buttocks, hands, and feet. During the physical examination, the vital signs include body temperature 39.0°C (102.3°F), heart rate 130/min, and respiratory rate 45/min. Ears, nose, and oral mucosa preserved their integrity, while the skin presents with diffuse blanching erythema and flaccid blisters with a positive Nikolsky’s sign. What is the most likely diagnosis in this patient?

A. Scarlet fever
B. Scalded skin syndrome
C. Impetigo
D. Pyoderma
resposta_gerada:
B

The clinical presentation is classic for Staphylococcal Scalded Skin Syndrome (SSSS). The key differentiating features are the presence of flaccid blisters, diffuse erythema, and a positive Nikolsky's sign (where the skin sloughs off with gentle rubbing), which indicates a superficial split within the epidermis. This distinguishes SSSS from toxic epidermal necrolysis or Stevens-Johnson syndrome, which typically involve mucous membranes (which are preserved in this case) and deeper skin detachment. Additionally, the sparing of the mucous membranes and the specific distribution of blisters (often starting around the buttocks and spreading) are characteristic of SSSS, which is caused by exfoliative toxins produced by *Staphylococcus aureus*. Scarlet fever presents with a sandpaper-like rash and strawberry tongue, impetigo typically presents with honey-colored crusts rather than widespread flaccid bullae, and pyoderma refers to a general term for skin infections rather than this specific acute systemic syndrome.

A 65-year-old man comes to the physician because of progressively worsening fatigue for 6 months. During this time, he has also had shortness of breath and palpitations on exertion. He has noticed blood in his stools on three separate occasions in the past 4 months. He has type 2 diabetes mellitus and end-stage renal disease. He drinks two to four beers daily. He does not smoke. His pulse is 95/min and blood pressure is 120/70 mm Hg. Examination shows pale conjunctivae. The abdomen is soft with no organomegaly. Rectal examination is unremarkable. His hemoglobin concentration is 7.2 g/dL, hematocrit is 32%, and mean corpuscular volume is 68 μm3. Which of the following is the most likely underlying cause of this patient's bleeding?

A. Inflammation in an outpouching of the colonic wall
B. Symptomatic enlargement of hemorrhoidal plexus
C. Chronic mucosal and submucosal inflammation of the colon
D. Arteriovenous malformation in the colonic wall
resposta_gerada:
D

This patient presents with iron deficiency anemia (low hemoglobin, low MCV) and overt rectal bleeding in the setting of end-stage renal disease (ESRD). While ESRD causes anemia primarily due to decreased erythropoietin production, the presence of visible blood in the stools suggests a concurrent gastrointestinal source of bleeding. In elderly patients with ESRD, the most common cause of lower gastrointestinal bleeding is colonic arteriovenous malformations (AVMs). These lesions are often asymptomatic until they bleed significantly, leading to anemia.

Option A describes diverticulosis, which is a common cause of painless lower GI bleeding in the elderly, but AVMs are statistically more frequent in patients with ESRD. Option B (hemorrhoids) typically causes bright red blood per rectum but rarely results in significant anemia or the degree of blood loss described here. Option C describes inflammatory bowel disease (like ulcerative colitis), which usually presents with diarrhea, abdominal pain, and mucosal inflammation, none of which are prominent in this vignette. Therefore, an AVM is the most likely underlying cause.
resposta_esperada: Arteriovenous malformation in the colonic wall

A bone marrow biopsy demonstrates 34% myeloblasts with Auer rods that are myeloperoxidase positive. What is best treatment option?

A. Ascorbic acid
B. Fresh frozen plasma
C. Retinoic acid
D. Zoledronic acid
resposta_gerada:
C

The patient's presentation of fever, bleeding, hepatosplenomegaly, and lymphadenopathy, combined with laboratory findings of pancytopenia (anemia, thrombocytopenia, and leukopenia) and coagulopathy (elevated PT/PTT, low fibrinogen, elevated D-dimer), is highly suggestive of acute leukemia with secondary disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC). The definitive diagnosis is confirmed by the bone marrow biopsy showing 34% myeloblasts with Auer rods and myeloperoxidase positivity, which is pathognomonic for Acute Myeloid Leukemia (AML).

Among the specific options provided:
*   **Ascorbic acid** is used for scurvy.
*   **Fresh frozen plasma** treats coagulopathy but does not address the underlying malignancy.
*   **Zoledronic acid** is a bisphosphonate used for hypercalcemia or bone metastases.
*   **Retinoic acid** (All-trans retinoic acid or ATRA) is a cornerstone of induction therapy for Acute Promyelocytic Leukemia (APL), a specific subtype of AML (FAB M3). APL is characterized by the presence of Auer rods (often in bundles) and carries a very high risk of fatal hemorrhage due to DIC, matching this patient's severe coagulopathy. While ATRA is specific to the APL subtype, it is the only option listed that represents a targeted treatment for AML. In the context of multiple-choice questions regarding AML with Auer rods and DIC, ATRA is the intended answer to distinguish it from supportive care or treatments for other conditions.

She has been living alone since her husband passed away 2 years ago. She has remained an active member of her retirement community's wine club; however, she stopped attending the meetings 3 weeks ago. She is generally able to her maintain her house, but her house appears more disorganized over the past 2 weeks. She generally drives short distances but avoids driving long distances as she occasionally gets lost when navigating new areas. She feels like her balance is getting worse, but she has not fallen. She has noticed increased urinary urgency over the past 8 months and has had 2 episodes of incontinence. Despite these changes, she reports feeling well. She drinks 4-6 glasses of wine per day. She was started on multiple medications for worsening anxiety by her psychiatrist 1 month ago. Her BMI is 31 kg/m^2. Her temperature is 99.8°F (37.7°C), blood pressure is 115/65 mmHg, pulse is 95/min, and respirations are 17/min. On examination, she is oriented to person and time but not place or situation. She does not seem to recognize her doctor despite knowing him for many years. She becomes somnolent intermittently throughout the interview. She can recall 0/3 words after 5 minutes. She has a low-frequency tremor in her right arm that increases in severity with deliberate movement. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis in this patient?

A. Alzheimer dementia
B. Delirium
C. Lewy body dementia
D. Normal pressure hydrocephalus
resposta_gerada:
B

The patient presents with an acute onset (over the past 2–3 weeks) of fluctuating mental status, evidenced by her somnolence, disorientation to place and situation, and inability to recall words. Crucially, she exhibits an acute change in attention and awareness, which is the hallmark of delirium. Several factors support this diagnosis over dementia: the rapid progression, the fluctuating course (somnolent intermittently), and the presence of clear precipitating causes such as alcohol use (4–6 glasses of wine daily), recent initiation of multiple anxiolytic medications, and urinary tract symptoms (urgency/incontinence). While her history includes tremor and balance issues suggestive of Parkinson's disease, the acute confusional state with fluctuating consciousness points to a superimposed delirium rather than the progressive decline seen in Alzheimer's, Lewy body dementia, or Normal pressure hydrocephalus.

A 45-year-old male with a history of diabetes and poorly controlled hypertension presents to his primary care physician for an annual check-up. He reports that he feels well and has no complaints. He takes enalapril and metformin. His temperature is 98.8°F (37.1°C), blood pressure is 155/90 mmHg, pulse is 80/min, and respirations are 16/min. His physician adds another anti-hypertensive medication to the patient’s regimen. One month later, the patient returns to the physician complaining of new onset lower extremity swelling. Which of the following medications was likely prescribed to this patient?

A. Metoprolol
B. Verapamil
C. Nifedipine
D. Hydrochlorthiazide
resposta_gerada:
C

The patient is a 45-year-old male with poorly controlled hypertension and diabetes. He is already taking an ACE inhibitor (enalapril) and a metformin. The new symptom of lower extremity swelling (peripheral edema) appearing one month after adding a new antihypertensive is a classic side effect of dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers. Among the choices, **Nifedipine** is a dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker. These drugs cause significant vasodilation of the precapillary arterioles, which increases hydrostatic pressure in the capillaries and leads to fluid leakage into the interstitial space, resulting in peripheral edema. This side effect is dose-dependent and occurs in a significant percentage of patients taking dihydropyridines like nifedipine, amlodipine, or felodipine.

In contrast, Metoprolol (a beta-blocker) and Verapamil (a non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker) are less likely to cause significant peripheral edema; Verapamil may actually reduce edema if used in combination with dihydropyridines. Hydrochlorothiazide (a thiazide diuretic) typically causes volume depletion and would not present with new onset swelling; in fact, it is often used to treat edema. Therefore, the clinical picture strongly points to the addition of a dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker.

A 29-year-old woman comes to the physician with high-grade fever, headache, and muscle pain. A week ago, she returned from India, where she was working with an NGO to build houses in rural areas. The patient took one dose of chloroquine one week before her trip. She also took a further dose during her trip. She has no history of a serious illness. Her temperature is 39.3°C (102.7°F), pulse is 102/min, respirations are 22/min, and blood pressure is 112/78 mm Hg. Physical examination shows jaundice. The abdomen is soft and nontender. The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities. Her hemoglobin concentration is 10 g/dL and a blood smear shows fragmented erythrocytes and occasional ring-shaped inclusion bodies within erythrocytes. Which of the following is the most likely cause of infection in this patient?

A. Plasmodium ovale
B. Plasmodium falciparum
C. Chikungunya virus
D. Hepatitis A virus
resposta_gerada:
B

The patient's presentation of high-grade fever, headache, muscle pain, jaundice, and anemia (hemoglobin 10 g/dL) following travel to India is highly suggestive of malaria. The key diagnostic clue is the blood smear finding of "ring-shaped inclusion bodies," which are characteristic of *Plasmodium* species. While *Plasmodium ovale* also presents with ring forms, it is typically associated with oval-shaped red blood cells and Schüffner's dots, and is less common in India compared to *P. falciparum*. *P. falciparum* is the most prevalent and dangerous species in India, often causing severe symptoms like jaundice (due to hemolysis) and cerebral involvement, though this patient currently lacks neurological signs. The presence of fragmented erythrocytes indicates hemolysis, consistent with severe malaria. Chikungunya virus causes fever and severe joint pain but does not cause ring forms on a blood smear or significant hemolytic anemia. Hepatitis A virus causes jaundice but would not present with ring forms or the acute febrile illness with hemolysis described here. Therefore, *Plasmodium falciparum* is the most likely cause.

This drug is used in the treatment of acute lymphoblastic leukemia, lymphomas, and some solid tumors. Its most important toxic side effect, and the one that limits its use as a chemotherapeutic agent, is a peripheral neuropathy. Paresthesias of the feet, hands, or both may occur within a few weeks of the beginning of treatment; with continued use of the drug, a progressive symmetrical neuropathy evolves (mainly sensory with reflex loss). Cranial nerves are affected less frequently, but ptosis and lateral rectus, facial, and vocal cord palsies have been observed. Autonomic nervous system function may also be affected: constipation and impotence are frequent complications; orthostatic hypotension, atonicity of the bladder, and adynamic ileus are less frequent. The polyneuropathy caused by vincristine is described more fully in Chap. 43. Inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion and seizures have been reported but are uncommon.

Neurotoxicity is second to myelosuppression as the dose-limiting toxicity of chemotherapeutic agents (Table 118-4). In this condition, damage to the lateral corticospinal tract on the left side causes ipsilateral (left-sided) spastic paralysis and loss of proprioception/vibration below the lesion. Damage to the spinothalamic tract, which carries pain and temperature sensation, results in contralateral (right-sided) loss of pain and temperature sensation starting 1-2 segments below the lesion. Additionally, damage to the descending sympathetic fibers in the lateral horn at the level of the lesion leads to ipsilateral (left-sided) Horner's syndrome (ptosis, miosis, anhidrosis).

The question asks for the statistical threshold used to conclude that two genetic loci (in this case, the CFTR gene and a novel mutation) are closely linked. In genetic linkage analysis, the LOD score (Logarithm of the Odds) compares the likelihood of observing the data if the loci are linked at a specific recombination fraction versus the likelihood if they are unlinked (recombination fraction = 0.5). A LOD score greater than 3 indicates that the observed data are 1000 times more likely if the loci are linked than if they are unlinked, which is the standard criterion for accepting linkage. Conversely, a LOD score less than -2 is typically used to reject linkage. Options A, B, and D represent values that do not provide sufficient statistical evidence to confirm linkage. Therefore, a LOD score > 3 is the correct indicator.

The patient presents with signs of severe hypovolemic shock (tachycardia, hypotension, delayed capillary refill, pale appearance) likely due to upper gastrointestinal bleeding from chronic alcohol use (spider angiomata, distended abdomen suggesting cirrhosis). In response to significant blood loss and decreased venous return, the body activates the sympathetic nervous system to maintain perfusion to vital organs. This results in increased heart rate, increased cardiac contractility, and a profound increase in systemic vascular resistance (SVR) via vasoconstriction. Consequently, the baroreceptors in the carotid sinus, which normally fire in proportion to blood pressure, detect the drop in pressure and significantly **decrease** their firing rate to trigger this compensatory sympathetic response. Therefore, compared to a healthy adult at rest, this patient's carotid baroreceptor firing activity is decreased. In contrast, SVR is increased (not decreased), cardiac inotropy is increased (not decreased), and fractional tissue oxygen extraction is typically increased (not decreased) as tissues attempt to compensate for reduced oxygen delivery.

The clinical presentation of a 14-year-old with gallstones, normocytic anemia, reticulocytosis, indirect hyperbilirubinemia, and a negative Coombs test is highly suggestive of hereditary spherocytosis. The key diagnostic clue provided is the osmotic fragility test showing increased fragility in hypotonic solution, which is the hallmark finding for hereditary spherocytosis. In this condition, red blood cells lose membrane surface area relative to their volume, becoming spherical and less deformable. Consequently, a peripheral blood smear in a patient with hereditary spherocytosis would characteristically show spherocytes (small, round RBCs lacking central pallor). Hypersegmented neutrophils are associated with megaloblastic anemia, sideroblasts with sideroblastic anemia, and dacrocytes with myelofibrosis or membrane defects like pyropoikilocytosis, none of which fit the specific combination of osmotic fragility and negative Coombs test described.

The patient ingested sodium fluoroacetate, a pesticide that is metabolized in the body to fluoroacetic acid, which is then converted to fluorocitrate. Fluorocitrate acts as a potent inhibitor of the enzyme aconitase in the Krebs cycle (citric acid cycle). Aconitase is responsible for converting citrate to isocitrate. When aconitase is inhibited, citrate cannot be further metabolized and consequently accumulates within the cells. This accumulation leads to a blockage of the entire cycle, preventing the production of downstream metabolites like isocitrate, alpha-ketoglutarate, succinate, fumarate, and malate, and ultimately halting ATP production, which explains the patient's decreased consciousness and convulsions. Therefore, the substance that accumulates is citrate.

The study design described recruits 30 patients with myocardial infarction (MI) and 60 healthy controls, which is a **case-control study**. In this design, the researchers compare the exposure history (educational status) between those with the disease and those without. The key statistical measure provided is the **odds ratio (OR) of 2.1** with a **95% confidence interval (CI) of 0.9–9.7**.

To determine statistical significance for an odds ratio, one must look at the confidence interval. If the 95% CI includes the value **1.0**, the result is **not statistically significant** at the p < 0.05 level. In this case, the interval ranges from 0.9 to 9.7, which clearly includes 1.0. Therefore, the observed association between low education and MI in this specific sample could be due to chance, and we cannot conclude that low education is a statistically significant risk factor based on these data. While the point estimate (2.1) suggests a potential trend, the lack of statistical significance means we cannot confirm the association. Option A correctly identifies that the association is not statistically significant and, consequently, that low education cannot be definitively labeled as a risk factor based on this study's results.
resposta_esperada: The association is not statistically significant, and low education is not a risk factor.

The patient is a 36-year-old male who underwent an exploratory laparotomy for a perforated duodenal ulcer. Twelve hours post-operatively, he presents with shortness of breath and reduced breath sounds over the left lung base. The clinical picture is highly suggestive of post-operative atelectasis. Atelectasis is a very common complication following abdominal surgery due to pain limiting deep breathing (splinting), anesthesia effects, and reduced lung volumes. The key findings supporting this diagnosis include the recent major surgery, the presence of reduced breath sounds localized to the lung base (consistent with collapse of the lower lobes), and the absence of other signs like fever (37.4°C is low-grade/normal), significant leukocytosis (10,600 is only mildly elevated), or calf tenderness (making DVT less likely). While he has a history of asthma, the localized finding of reduced breath sounds and the immediate post-operative timing make atelectasis the most likely cause rather than an asthma exacerbation. Pneumonitis would typically present with more diffuse infiltrates and higher fever, and pulmonary embolism is less likely given the lack of calf tenderness and the specific localized lung findings.

In cases of hypercalcemia of malignancy, bisphosphonates (such as alendronate, pamidronate, or zoledronic acid) are the standard of care for long-term management to inhibit osteoclast-mediated bone resorption and lower serum calcium levels. **Justification:** The patient is presenting with classic signs of **nocturnal hypoglycemia** (waking up with sweating, tremors, and weakness) but has a **high morning blood glucose**. This phenomenon is known as the **Somogyi effect**. It occurs when insulin levels are too high during the night, causing hypoglycemia, which triggers a counter-regulatory hormone response (release of glucagon, epinephrine, cortisol, and growth hormone) that causes rebound hyperglycemia by the morning. The optimal intervention is to **reduce the daily insulin dose** (specifically the evening or bedtime long-acting insulin) to prevent the initial nocturnal hypoglycemia. Increasing the dose (Option C) would worsen the night-time lows. Adding pramlintide (Option B) would further lower glucose and is generally not indicated for this specific rebound pattern without addressing the hypoglycemia first. Reassurance (Option A) is inappropriate given the dangerous nature of recurrent hypoglycemia.

The patient presents with the classic triad of hemoptysis, diffuse muscle pain (myositis), and shortness of breath (dyspnea), accompanied by pulmonary crackles and renal involvement (elevated creatinine, proteinuria, hematuria). This clinical picture is highly suggestive of Goodpasture syndrome (anti-glomerular basement membrane disease) or potentially a severe vasculitis like Granulomatosis with Polyangiitis (GPA). Both conditions involve autoimmune-mediated damage to the lungs and kidneys. The immediate life-threatening concern is alveolar hemorrhage causing hypoxia. The standard of care for severe, life-threatening pulmonary-renal syndromes induced by autoantibodies involves aggressive immunosuppression to halt antibody production and removal of circulating pathogenic antibodies. Therefore, the most appropriate initial treatment regimen includes high-dose corticosteroids (Methylprednisolone) to rapidly suppress inflammation, cyclophosphamide for long-term immunosuppression, and plasmapheresis to mechanically remove the circulating anti-GBM antibodies or ANCA complexes. While plasmapheresis is sometimes debated in ANCA vasculitis, it is a cornerstone of therapy in Goodpasture syndrome and severe pulmonary hemorrhage, making the combination of all three the most comprehensive and appropriate choice among the options provided.

Sodium nitroprusside is a potent, balanced vasodilator that affects both the arterial and venous systems. By dilating veins, it reduces venous return to the heart, thereby decreasing preload. **Justification:** The patient is presenting with anaphylactic shock (hypotension, bronchospasm, angioedema) that is refractory to initial first-line treatments (epinephrine and fluids). The patient's history of taking **labetalol** (a non-selective beta-blocker with alpha-blocking activity) is the critical factor here. Beta-blockers can antagonize the effects of epinephrine by blocking beta-adrenergic receptors, leading to "refractory anaphylaxis" where standard doses of epinephrine fail to raise blood pressure. In such cases, the next best step is to administer a vasopressor that acts primarily on alpha-adrenergic receptors to cause vasoconstriction and increase systemic vascular resistance, bypassing the blocked beta-receptors. **Norepinephrine** is the preferred agent in this scenario because it has potent alpha-1 agonist activity (causing vasoconstriction) and minimal beta-2 activity, making it effective even in the presence of beta-blockade. While dopamine (Option A) has some alpha activity, norepinephrine is generally preferred in anaphylactic shock due to its more predictable hemodynamic profile and lower risk of tachyarrhythmias. Glucagon (Option B) is typically reserved for beta-blocker overdose causing cardiogenic shock (bradycardia/hypotension), not primarily for anaphylaxis, though it can be considered if the patient is in profound beta-blocker toxicity; however, norepinephrine is the standard immediate rescue for refractory anaphylactic hypotension. Dexamethasone (Option C) is too slow-acting to treat acute hemodynamic instability. The provided context explicitly states to "give pressors (dopamine or norepinephrine)" when hypotension persists, supporting the use of norepinephrine.

The clinical presentation of a young woman with palpitations, chest pain, fine tremor, digital swelling (thyroid acropachy), lid retraction, and a systolic ejection murmur is classic for **thyrotoxicosis** (hyperthyroidism), likely due to Graves' disease. The irregularly irregular pulse indicates atrial fibrillation secondary to the hypermetabolic state.

In patients with thyrotoxicosis presenting with atrial fibrillation, the primary goal of pharmacotherapy is to control the heart rate and manage the underlying thyroid dysfunction. **Propranolol**, a non-selective beta-blocker, is the drug of choice in this scenario for two reasons:
1.  It effectively controls the rapid ventricular response associated with atrial fibrillation.
2.  It has intrinsic thyroid-blocking properties (inhibits peripheral conversion of T4 to T3) and can alleviate adrenergic symptoms like tremor and palpitations while waiting for definitive thyroid treatment (antithyroid drugs or radioactive iodine).

Other options are less appropriate:
*   **Digoxin** is less effective in hyperthyroid patients because the increased sympathetic tone and shortened action potential duration render the heart less responsive to its effects.
*   **Amiodarone** contains a high iodine load, which can worsen or precipitate thyrotoxicosis (Jod-Basedow effect), making it a poor choice unless absolutely necessary and monitored closely.
*   **Warfarin** is an anticoagulant used to prevent stroke in atrial fibrillation but does not treat the arrhythmia itself or the underlying cause. While anticoagulation may be considered based on CHA2DS2-VASc score, it is not the primary therapy for the symptomatic palpitations and rate control described.

Background:
Some patients with severe asthma have frequent exacerbations associated with persistent eosinophilic inflammation despite continuous treatment with high-dose inhaled glucocorticoids with or without oral glucocorticoids.
Methods:
In this randomized, double-blind clinical trial we assigned 576 patients with recurrent asthma exacerbations and evidence of eosinophilic inflammation despite high doses of inhaled glucocorticoids to one of three study groups. Patients were assigned to receive mepolizumab, a humanized monoclonal antibody against interleukin-5, which was administered as either a 75-mg intravenous dose or a 100-mg subcutaneous dose or placebo every 4 weeks for 32 weeks. The primary outcome was the rate of exacerbations. Other outcomes included the forced expiratory volume in 1 second (FEV1) and scores on the St. George’s Respiratory Questionnaire (SGRQ) and the 5-item Asthma Control Questionnaire (ACQ-5).
Results:
The rate of exacerbations was reduced by 47% (95% confidence interval [CI], 29 to 61) among patients receiving intravenous mepolizumab and by 53% (95% CI, 37 to 65) among those receiving subcutaneous mepolizumab, as compared with those receiving placebo (p<0.001 for both comparisons). Exacerbations necessitating an emergency department visit or hospitalization were reduced by 32% in the group receiving intravenous mepolizumab and by 61% in the group receiving subcutaneous mepolizumab. At week 32, the mean increase from baseline in FEV1 was 100 ml greater in patients receiving intravenous mepolizumab than in those receiving placebo (p=0.02) and 98 ml greater in patients receiving subcutaneous mepolizumab than in those receiving placebo (p=0.03). The improvement from baseline in the SGRQ score was 6.4 points and 7.0 points greater in the intravenous and subcutaneous mepolizumab groups, respectively than in the placebo group, and the improvement in the ACQ-5 score was 0.42 points and 0.44 points greater in the two mepolizumab groups, respectively than in the placebo group (p<0.001 for all comparisons).
Conclusions:
Mepolizumab administered either intravenously or subcutaneously significantly reduced asthma exacerbations and was associated with improvements in markers of asthma control.

The clinical vignette describes a drug that "prevents further bone resorption" (the mechanism of action of bisphosphonates) and "reduces her risk of developing breast cancer." Bisphosphonates are known to inhibit osteoclast-mediated bone resorption and have been associated with a reduced risk of breast cancer recurrence or development in postmenopausal women.

A well-documented, albeit rare, adverse effect of bisphosphonate therapy is **osteonecrosis of the jaw (ONJ)**, which is not listed as an option. However, bisphosphonates are also associated with an increased risk of **atypical femoral fractures** and, more commonly in the context of general pharmacology questions regarding this class, there is often confusion or specific testing regarding other classes. Let's re-evaluate the drug choice based on the "reduces risk of breast cancer" clue.

Actually, the drug that fits the description of preventing bone resorption and reducing breast cancer risk is **Raloxifene**. Raloxifene is a Selective Estrogen Receptor Modulator (SERM).
*   **Mechanism:** It acts as an estrogen agonist on bone (preventing resorption) and an antagonist on breast tissue (reducing cancer risk).
*   **Adverse Effects:** The most significant and common serious adverse effect of Raloxifene is an increased risk of **venous thromboembolism (VTE)**, which includes **deep vein thrombosis (DVT)** and pulmonary embolism.

Let's verify the other options:

*   B. Osteosarcoma: Associated with high-dose radiation or nitrogen mustards, not these drugs.
*   C. Hypercholesterolemia: Raloxifene actually has a favorable effect on lipids (lowers LDL), unlike some other drugs.
*   D. Deep vein thrombosis: This is the classic, high-yield adverse effect associated with SERMs like Raloxifene and Tamoxifen.

Therefore, the drug is Raloxifene, and the increased risk is Deep Vein Thrombosis.

In Parkinson and other extrapyramidal diseases associated with rigidity of muscles, one observes a rather different disturbance of articulation, characterized by rapid mumbling and cluttered utterance and slurring of words and syllables. The voice is low-pitched and monotonous, lacking both inflection and volume (hypophonia), and trailing off in volume at the ends of sentences. Words are spoken hastily and run together in a pattern that is almost the opposite of the slowed pattern of spastic dysarthria. In advanced cases, speech is whispered and almost unintelligible. It may happen that the patient finds it impossible to talk while walking but can speak better if standing still, sitting, or lying down. In the extrapyramidal disorder of progressive supranuclear palsy, the dysarthria and dysphonia tend instead to be spastic in nature.

The first neurologic manifestations are most often extrapyramidal with a proclivity to affect the oropharyngeal musculature. The typical presentations are tremor of a limb or of the head and generalized slowness of movement (i.e., a parkinsonian syndrome); or slowness of movement of the tongue, lips, pharynx, larynx, and jaws, resulting in dysarthria, dysphagia, and hoarseness; or there may be slowness of finger movement and occasionally choreic movements or dystonic postures of the limbs. Often the mouth is held slightly open in the early stage of the disease. Exceptionally, an abnormality of behavior (argumentativeness, impulsiveness, excessive emotionality, depression, delusions) or a gradual impairment of intellectual faculties precedes other neurologic signs by a year or more (see Starosta-Rubinstein et al).

Its most important toxic side effect, and the one that limits its use as a chemotherapeutic agent, is a peripheral neuropathy. Paresthesias of the feet, hands, or both may occur within a few weeks of the beginning of treatment; with continued use of the drug, a progressive symmetrical neuropathy evolves (mainly sensory with reflex loss). Cranial nerves are affected less frequently, but ptosis and lateral rectus, facial, and vocal cord palsies have been observed. Autonomic nervous system function may also be affected: constipation and impotence are frequent complications; orthostatic hypotension, atonicity of the bladder, and adynamic ileus are less frequent. Cisplatin causes large fiber sensory loss resulting in sensory ataxia but little cutaneous sensory loss and no weakness. The taxanes also cause a predominately sensory neuropathy. Agents such as bortezomib and thalidomide also cause neuropathy.

Thus, niacin causes a decrease in liver TAG synthesis, which is required for very-low-density lipoprotein ([VLDL] see p. 230) production. nicotinic acid Nicotinic acid, or niacin, is a B-complex vitamin that has been used as a lipid-modifying agent for more than five decades.
