The presentation of sarcoidosis ranges from patients who are asymptomatic to those with organ failure. It is unclear how often sarcoidosis is asymptomatic. In countries where routine chest roentgenogram screening is performed, 20–30% of pulmonary cases are detected in asymptomatic individuals. The inability to screen for other asymptomatic forms of the disease would suggest that as many as one-third of sarcoidosis patients are asymptomatic. Respiratory complaints including cough and dyspnea are the most common presenting symptoms. In many cases, the patient presents with a 2-to 4-week history of these symptoms. Unfortunately, due to the nonspecific nature of pulmonary symptoms, the patient may see physicians for up to a year before a diagnosis is confirmed. For these patients, the diagnosis of sarcoidosis is usually only suggested when a chest roentgenogram is performed.

Severe cold injury in an infant is manifested by acidosis, hypoxia, hypoglycemia, apnea, bradycardia, pulmonary hemorrhage, and a pink skin color. The color is caused by trapping of oxygenated hemoglobin in the cutaneous capillaries. Many of these infants appear dead, but most respond to treatment and recover. Milder degrees of cold injury in the delivery room may contribute to metabolic acidosis and hypoxia after birth. Conversely, hypoxia delays heat generation in cold-stressed infants. Treatment of severe hypothermia should involve resuscitation and rapid warming of core (e.g., lung and stomach) and external surfaces. Fluid resuscitation also is needed to treat hypovolemia seen in many of these infants. Background:
Some patients with severe asthma have frequent exacerbations associated with persistent eosinophilic inflammation despite continuous treatment with high-dose inhaled glucocorticoids with or without oral glucocorticoids.
Methods:
In this randomized, double-blind clinical trial we assigned 576 patients with recurrent asthma exacerbations and evidence of eosinophilic inflammation despite high doses of inhaled glucocorticoids to one of three study groups. Patients were assigned to receive mepolizumab, a humanized monoclonal antibody against interleukin-5, which was administered as either a 75-mg intravenous dose or a 100-mg subcutaneous dose or placebo every 4 weeks for 32 weeks. The primary outcome was the rate of exacerbations. Other outcomes included the forced expiratory volume in 1 second (FEV1) and scores on the St. George’s Respiratory Questionnaire (SGRQ) and the 5-item Asthma Control Questionnaire (ACQ-5).
Results:
The rate of exacerbations was reduced by 47% (95% confidence interval [CI], 29 to 61) among patients receiving intravenous mepolizumab and by 53% (95% CI, 37 to 65) among those receiving subcutaneous mepolizumab, as compared with those receiving placebo (p<0.001 for both comparisons). Exacerbations necessitating an emergency department visit or hospitalization were reduced by 32% in the group receiving intravenous mepolizumab and by 61% in the group receiving subcutaneous mepolizumab. At week 32, the mean increase from baseline in FEV1 was 100 ml greater in patients receiving intravenous mepolizumab than in those receiving placebo (p=0.02) and 98 ml greater in patients receiving subcutaneous mepolizumab than in those receiving placebo (p=0.03). The improvement from baseline in the SGRQ score was 6.4 points and 7.0 points greater in the intravenous and subcutaneous mepolizumab groups, respectively than in the placebo group, and the improvement in the ACQ-5 score was 0.42 points and 0.44 points greater in the two mepolizumab groups, respectively than in the placebo group (p<0.001 for all comparisons).
Conclusions:
Mepolizumab administered either intravenously or subcutaneously significantly reduced asthma exacerbations and was associated with improvements in markers of asthma control.

The maneuver of standing from a supine position causes venous pooling in the lower extremities due to gravity, which significantly decreases venous return (preload) to the heart. This reduction in blood volume returning to the left ventricle leads to a shorter duration of diastole, thereby reducing the time available for ventricular filling (diastolic filling time). Consequently, stroke volume decreases, which can intensify the murmur associated with aortic stenosis in this patient. Options A and B are incorrect because standing decreases, rather than increases, right atrial and pulmonary capillary wedge pressures due to reduced preload. In Parkinson and other extrapyramidal diseases associated with rigidity of muscles, one observes a rather different disturbance of articulation, characterized by rapid mumbling and cluttered utterance and slurring of words and syllables. The voice is low-pitched and monotonous, lacking both inflection and volume (hypophonia), and trailing off in volume at the ends of sentences. Words are spoken hastily and run together in a pattern that is almost the opposite of the slowed pattern of spastic dysarthria. In advanced cases, speech is whispered and almost unintelligible. It may happen that the patient finds it impossible to talk while walking but can speak better if standing still, sitting, or lying down. In the extrapyramidal disorder of progressive supranuclear palsy, the dysarthria and dysphonia tend instead to be spastic in nature.

The first neurologic manifestations are most often extrapyramidal with a proclivity to affect the oropharyngeal musculature. The typical presentations are tremor of a limb or of the head and generalized slowness of movement (i.e., a parkinsonian syndrome); or slowness of movement of the tongue, lips, pharynx, larynx, and jaws, resulting in dysarthria, dysphagia, and hoarseness; or there may be slowness of finger movement and occasionally choreic movements or dystonic postures of the limbs. Often the mouth is held slightly open in the early stage of the disease. Exceptionally, an abnormality of behavior (argumentativeness, impulsiveness, excessive emotionality, depression, delusions) or a gradual impairment of intellectual faculties precedes other neurologic signs by a year or more (see Starosta-Rubinstein et al).

Schizophrenia is a heterogeneous syndrome characterized by perturbations of language, perception, thinking, social activity, affect, and volition. There are no pathognomonic features. The syndrome commonly begins in late adolescence, has an insidious (and less commonly acute) onset, and, often, a poor outcome, progressing from social withdrawal and perceptual distortions to recurrent delusions and hallucinations. Patients may present with positive symptoms (such as conceptual disorganization, delusions, or hallucinations) or negative symptoms (loss of function, anhedonia, decreased emotional expression, impaired concentration, and diminished social engagement) and must have at least two of these for a 1-month period and continuous signs for at least 6 months to meet formal diagnostic criteria. contextos_recuperados: Insidiously, or after some unusual activity, raising the question of trauma, especially if it happens in the work-place, the patient develops aching pain in the low back, increased by certain movements and attended by stiffness. The pain may additionally have a restricted radiation into the buttocks and posterior thigh, thereby simulating root compression. There are no motor, sensory, or reflex abnormalities. Imaging usually reveals some combination of osteoarthropathy, changes in vertebral discs, osteoarthritic changes in apophyseal joints, and sometimes osteoporosis or slight spondylosis, or they may be entirely normal. Treatment with short-duration bed rest, analgesics, and physiotherapy, as outlined for acute strains, helps to relieve the symptoms, and the majority of patients recover within a few weeks, only to have a recurrence of similar pains in the future.

Conventional radiographs of the lumbar spine in the anteroposterior, lateral, and oblique planes (preferably with the patient standing) are not very useful in the routine evaluation of low back pain and sciatica but they can disclose some information. Readily demonstrable in plain films are narrowing of the intervertebral disc spaces, bony facetal or vertebral overgrowth, displacement of vertebral bodies (spondylolisthesis), compression and other fractures of the spine, and most importantly, unsuspected infiltration of bone by cancer or myeloma. However, in cases of suspected disc herniation or tumor infiltration of the spinal canal, one generally proceeds directly to MRI if subsequent action is to be taken.

The cause of low back pain occasionally remains unclear. Some patients have had multiple operations for disk disease but have persistent pain and disability. The original indications for surgery may have been questionable, with back pain only, no definite neurologic signs, or a minor disk bulge noted on CT or MRI. Scoring systems based on neurologic signs, psychological factors, physiologic studies, and imaging studies have been devised to minimize the likelihood of unsuccessful surgery. HEALTH CARE FOR POPuLATIONS OF BACK PAIN PATIENTS: A CLINICAL CARE SYSTEMS VIEW There are increasing pressures to contain health care costs, especially when expensive care is not based on sound evidence. Physicians, patients, the insurance industry, and government providers of health care will need to work together to ensure cost-effective care for patients with back pain.

Back pain is the most common neurologic symptom in patients with systemic cancer and is the presenting symptom in 20%. The cause is usually vertebral body metastasis but can also result from spread of cancer through the intervertebral foramen (especially with lymphoma), from carcinomatous meningitis, or from metastasis to the spinal cord. Cancer-related back pain tends to be constant, dull, unrelieved by rest, and worse at night. By contrast, mechanical low back pain usually improves with rest. MRI, CT, and CT myelography are the studies of choice when spinal metastasis is suspected. Once a metastasis is found, imaging of the entire spine reveals additional tumor deposits in one-third of patients. MRI is preferred for soft tissue definition, but the most rapidly available imaging modality is best because the patient’s condition may worsen quickly without intervention. This drug is used in the treatment of acute lymphoblastic leukemia, lymphomas, and some solid tumors. Its most important toxic side effect, and the one that limits its use as a chemotherapeutic agent, is a peripheral neuropathy. Paresthesias of the feet, hands, or both may occur within a few weeks of the beginning of treatment; with continued use of the drug, a progressive symmetrical neuropathy evolves (mainly sensory with reflex loss). Cranial nerves are affected less frequently, but ptosis and lateral rectus, facial, and vocal cord palsies have been observed. Autonomic nervous system function may also be affected: constipation and impotence are frequent complications; orthostatic hypotension, atonicity of the bladder, and adynamic ileus are less frequent. The polyneuropathy caused by vincristine is described more fully in Chap. 43. Inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion and seizures have been reported but are uncommon.

Neurotoxicity is second to myelosuppression as the dose-limiting toxicity of chemotherapeutic agents (Table 118-4). Chemotherapy causes peripheral neuropathy from a number of commonly used agents, and the type of neuropathy can differ, depending on the drug. Vincristine causes paresthesias but little sensory loss and is associated with motor dysfunction, autonomic impairment (frequently ileus), and rarely cranial nerve compromise. Cisplatin causes large fiber sensory loss resulting in sensory ataxia but little cutaneous sensory loss and no weakness. The taxanes also cause a predominately sensory neuropathy. Agents such as bortezomib and thalidomide also cause neuropathy.

The patient presents with Brown-Séquard syndrome (hemisection of the spinal cord) following a left C5 injury. This condition causes ipsilateral (left) motor paralysis and loss of proprioception, while the spinothalamic tract, which carries pain and temperature sensation, crosses over shortly after entering the cord. Consequently, a left-sided lesion results in contralateral (right-sided) loss of pain and temperature sensation (analgesia) below the level of the lesion. Option A is incorrect because paralysis at the exact level of the lesion is typically flaccid, not spastic (spasticity occurs below the lesion). Option B is incorrect because Horner's syndrome is ipsilateral to the lesion (left-sided), not right-sided. Option C is incorrect because corticospinal tract involvement is ipsilateral. Therefore, right-sided analgesia is the correct finding.

Cystic fibrosis (CF) is an autosomal recessive disorder that is the most common life-limiting genetic disease in whites. In the United States, the incidence of CF is approximately 1 in 3200 whites, 1 in 15,000 African Americans, and 1 in 31,000 persons of Asian heritage. The gene for CF, located on the long arm of chromosome 7, encodes for a polypeptide, the cystic fibrosis transmembrane regulator (CFTR), a chloride channel located on the apical surface of epithelial cells. CFTR is important for the proper movement of salt and water across cell membranes and maintaining the appropriate composition of various secretions, especially in the airways, liver, and pancreas. The most common mutation is a deletion of three base pairs resulting in the absence of phenylalanine at the 508 position (ΔF508). More than 1500 mutations of the CFTR gene have been identified.

The LOD (logarithm of the odds) score is the standard statistical metric used to evaluate genetic linkage. A score greater than 3 indicates that the odds in favor of linkage are 1000:1, which is the widely accepted threshold for declaring two loci to be closely linked. Scores below 3 (such as <1, <2, or =0) do not provide sufficient evidence to confirm linkage.

The patient presents with classic signs of primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison's disease), including fatigue, weight loss, hypotension, abdominal pain, and characteristic hyperpigmentation (bronze skin). The clinical presentation of a large, pedunculated tumor in the left atrium is classic for a cardiac myxoma. These tumors are highly mobile and can prolapse through the mitral valve into the left ventricle during diastole, causing acute obstruction of blood flow. This mechanical obstruction can lead to sudden hemodynamic collapse, syncope, or acute arterial occlusion (such as stroke or limb ischemia) if tumor fragments embolize. While sudden cardiac death (Option B) is a potential complication due to arrhythmias or severe obstruction, acute arterial occlusion is the most frequent and characteristic embolic event associated with left atrial myxomas, making it the primary risk to identify. Abrupt hypotension (Option A) is a consequence of the obstruction but "acute arterial occlusion" more specifically describes the embolic nature of the risk.

Patients with type II diabetes are at increased risk for diabetic neuropathy and peripheral arterial disease, which significantly elevate the risk of foot ulcers and subsequent amputations. Clinical guidelines, such as those from the American Diabetes Association (ADA), recommend that all patients with diabetes receive a comprehensive foot examination at least annually. This exam assesses sensation (monofilament testing), pulses, skin integrity, and deformities. While patients are also advised to perform daily foot inspections (Option C), the specific clinical screening measure mandated by guidelines is the annual comprehensive exam performed by a healthcare provider. Urinalysis is typically recommended annually, not every 6 months (Option A), and the meningococcal vaccine is not routinely recommended for all diabetic patients unless they have specific risk factors or are undergoing splenectomy (Option D).

nicotinic acid Nicotinic acid, or niacin, is a B-complex vitamin that has been used as a lipid-modifying agent for more than five decades. The patient presents with signs of severe hypovolemic shock (tachycardia, hypotension, delayed capillary refill) likely due to upper gastrointestinal bleeding from chronic alcohol use (esophageal varices). In response to hypotension, the body activates the sympathetic nervous system to maintain perfusion. This leads to increased heart rate, increased cardiac contractility, and, crucially, a significant increase in systemic vascular resistance (SVR) via vasoconstriction. Consequently, the baroreceptors in the carotid sinus, which normally fire in proportion to blood pressure, detect the low pressure and **decrease** their firing rate to signal the need for compensatory mechanisms. Therefore, compared to a healthy adult with normal blood pressure, this patient has decreased carotid baroreceptor firing activity. Options A is incorrect because SVR is increased, not decreased. Option B is incorrect because tissue oxygen extraction is typically increased in shock to compensate for low flow. Option D is incorrect because cardiac inotropy is increased due to sympathetic stimulation.

The recurrent laryngeal nerve runs in close proximity to the inferior thyroid artery and the thyroid gland itself. During a thyroidectomy, particularly when ligating the inferior thyroid arteries, there is a significant risk of iatrogenic injury to this nerve. Damage to the recurrent laryngeal nerve results in paralysis or paresis of the intrinsic muscles of the larynx (except the cricothyroid), leading to vocal cord dysfunction and the classic symptom of hoarseness. The other options are less likely: the internal laryngeal nerve is involved in sensation above the vocal cords, the external laryngeal nerve innervates the cricothyroid muscle (whose injury causes a weak, breathy voice rather than typical hoarseness), and laryngeal edema is not a direct consequence of arterial ligation.

The patient's presentation of confusion, lethargy, asterixis, and altered mental status in the context of known liver cirrhosis is classic for hepatic encephalopathy. A 40-year-old man presents to the clinic with complaints of increased bilateral pain in his knees. The pain developed over time and now limits his mobility. He states that the pain is worse at the end of the day, though he does have some early-morning stiffness lasting about 20 minutes. He used to have some success with over-the-counter NSAIDs; however, they no longer help. The patient also has been taking metformin for the past 2 years and is severely obese, with a BMI of 41 kg/m2. Additionally, he states that he has felt increasingly tired during the day, often dozes off during work, and no longer feels refreshed when he wakes up in the morning. Upon examination, there is no tenderness on palpation or erythema; however, some crepitus is felt. He has no other complaints but has a family history of rheumatoid arthritis (RA) on his mother’s side. B. Excess weight

contextos_recuperados: OA is the most common cause of chronic knee pain in persons over age 45, but the differential diagnosis is long. Inflammatory arthritis is likely if there is prolonged morning stiffness and many other joints are affected. Bursitis occurs commonly around knees and hips. A physical examination should focus on whether tenderness is over the joint line (at the junction of the two bones around which the joint is articulating) or is outside of it. Anserine bursitis, medial and distal to the knee, is an extremely common cause of chronic knee pain that may respond to a glucocorticoid injection. Prominent nocturnal pain in the absence of end-stage OA merits a distinct workup. For hip pain, OA can be detected by loss of internal rotation on passive movement, and pain isolated to an area lateral to the hip joint usually reflects the presence of trochanteric bursitis. No blood tests are routinely indicated for workup of patients with OA unless symptoms and signs suggest inflammatory arthritis.

Knee pain may result from intraarticular (OA, RA) or periarticular (anserine bursitis, collateral ligament strain) processes or be referred from hip pathology. A careful history should delineate the chronology of the knee complaint and whether there are predisposing conditions, trauma, or medications that might underlie the complaint. For example, patellofemoral disease (e.g., OA) may cause anterior knee pain that worsens with climbing stairs. Observation of the patient’s gait is also important. The knee should be carefully inspected in the upright (weight-bearing) and supine positions for swelling, erythema, malalignment, visible trauma, muscle wasting, and leg length discrepancy. The most common malalignment in the knee is genu varum (bowlegs) or genu valgum (knock-knees) resulting from asymmetric cartilage loss medially or laterally. Bony swelling of the knee joint commonly results from hypertrophic osseous changes seen with disorders such as OA and neuropathic arthropathy.

B. Excess weight

The patient's clinical presentation—bilateral knee pain worsening with activity, short morning stiffness (<30 minutes), crepitus, and absence of inflammatory signs (erythema, warmth)—is classic for osteoarthritis (OA). While the patient has a family history of rheumatoid arthritis, the lack of prolonged morning stiffness and inflammatory markers makes RA unlikely. The patient's severe obesity (BMI 41 kg/m²) is a primary mechanical risk factor for OA, causing increased stress on weight-bearing joints. Furthermore, the associated fatigue and daytime sleepiness are likely secondary to poor sleep quality caused by obesity-related conditions (such as sleep apnea) and chronic pain, rather than medication side effects, infection, or malignancy. Therefore, excess weight is the underlying cause of both the joint pathology and the systemic complaints.

Available @ StudentConsult.com The most common clinical presentation of Hodgkin disease is painless, firm lymphadenopathy often confined to one or two lymph node areas, usually the supraclavicular and cervical nodes. Mediastinal lymphadenopathy producing cough or shortness of breath is another frequent initial presentation. The presence of one of three B symptoms has prognostic value: fever (>38° C for 3 consecutive days), drenching night sweats, and unintentional weight loss of 10% or more within 6 months of diagnosis. The sporadic (North American) form of Burkitt lymphoma more commonly has an abdominal presentation (typically with pain), whereas the endemic (African) form frequently presents with tumors of the jaw. The anterior mediastinum and cervical nodes are the usual primary sites for T-cell lymphomas. These lymphomas may cause airway or superior vena cava obstruction, pleural effusion, or both.

The presentation of sarcoidosis ranges from patients who are asymptomatic to those with organ failure. It is unclear how often sarcoidosis is asymptomatic. In countries where routine chest roentgenogram screening is performed, 20–30% of pulmonary cases are detected in asymptomatic individuals. The inability to screen for other asymptomatic forms of the disease would suggest that as many as one-third of sarcoidosis patients are asymptomatic. Respiratory complaints including cough and dyspnea are the most common presenting symptoms. In many cases, the patient presents with a 2-to 4-week history of these symptoms. Unfortunately, due to the nonspecific nature of pulmonary symptoms, the patient may see physicians for up to a year before a diagnosis is confirmed. For these patients, the diagnosis of sarcoidosis is usually only suggested when a chest roentgenogram is performed.

The clinical presentation typically consists of months or years of throat clearing, nagging cough, and slowly progressive fatigue. In the absence of a positive Coombs test and blood group differences between the mother and fetus, other causes of non-immune hemolysis must be considered. The patient's presentation of hemolytic anemia (normocytic anemia, reticulocytosis, indirect hyperbilirubinemia) with a negative Coombs test and increased osmotic fragility is diagnostic for Hereditary Spherocytosis. In this condition, red blood cells lose membrane surface area, causing them to become spherical and less deformable, which leads to their premature destruction in the spleen. Consequently, a peripheral blood smear would characteristically reveal spherocytes. The other options are incorrect: hypersegmented neutrophils are seen in megaloblastic anemia, sideroblasts in sideroblastic anemia, and dacrocytes in myelofibrosis or membrane defects like hereditary pyropoikilocytosis, none of which fit the specific combination of negative Coombs and increased osmotic fragility.

The clinical scenario describes the treatment of chronic hepatitis C with interferon-α combined with ribavirin, which was the standard of care prior to direct-acting antivirals. The inferior vena cava (IVC) is a major retroperitoneal vessel that ascends along the right side of the vertebral column, passing anterior to the L1-L2 vertebrae and continuing downward. One concern is that physicians may develop a shift-worker mentality that undermines their dedication to the well-being of patients. In some cases, trainees could provide an irreplaceable benefit to a patient or family by going beyond work-hour limits, especially if there is rapport with the patient or family that is not easily transferred to another provider. The patient is experiencing anaphylactic shock that is refractory to initial first-line treatments (intramuscular epinephrine and aggressive fluid resuscitation), evidenced by persistent hypotension (90/55 mm Hg). According to standard emergency guidelines for anaphylaxis, when hypotension persists despite fluids and epinephrine, the administration of vasopressors is indicated. Norepinephrine is the preferred agent in this scenario due to its potent alpha-adrenergic effects which effectively increase systemic vascular resistance without the significant arrhythmogenic risk associated with dopamine. While the patient is on labetalol (a beta-blocker), which can blunt the response to epinephrine, the immediate life-threat remains the distributive shock of anaphylaxis, making norepinephrine the most appropriate next step among the choices provided. Glucagon is typically reserved for beta-blocker overdose or refractory anaphylaxis specifically when catecholamines are ineffective, but norepinephrine is the standard first-line pressor for refractory anaphylactic shock. Dexamethasone acts too slowly for acute hemodynamic stabilization.

The patient's presentation of dyspnea, elevated JVP, and bilateral lower extremity edema following a myocardial infarction is classic for congestive heart failure. In this condition, the heart's inability to pump effectively causes blood to back up into the venous system, increasing venous hydrostatic pressure. This elevated pressure is transmitted backward to the capillaries, increasing capillary pressure and forcing fluid out into the interstitial space, which results in edema. This mechanism aligns with Option A, whereas the other options describe different etiologies (e.g., hypoalbuminemia or inflammation) not supported by the clinical picture of volume overload and elevated JVP.

The patient presents with classic signs of cerebellar dysfunction, including a wide-based gait, inability to stand with feet together (ataxia), and impaired rapid alternating movements (dysdiadochokinesia). While the patient has a history of heavy alcohol use, which puts him at risk for thiamine deficiency, the specific neurological findings described are localized to the cerebellum. Therefore, the most likely cause of his specific motor symptoms is cerebellar degeneration, a known complication of chronic alcoholism.

Severe cold injury in an infant is manifested by acidosis, hypoxia, hypoglycemia, apnea, bradycardia, pulmonary hemorrhage, and a pink skin color. The color is caused by trapping of oxygenated hemoglobin in the cutaneous capillaries. Many of these infants appear dead, but most respond to treatment and recover. Milder degrees of cold injury in the delivery room may contribute to metabolic acidosis and hypoxia after birth. Conversely, hypoxia delays heat generation in cold-stressed infants. Treatment of severe hypothermia should involve resuscitation and rapid warming of core (e.g., lung and stomach) and external surfaces. Fluid resuscitation also is needed to treat hypovolemia seen in many of these infants. Reduced core temperature (32° C to 35° C) in the immediate newborn period often requires only external warming with a radiant warmer, incubator, or both.

The clinical presentation of white plaques on the tongue and mouth that are KOH-positive is diagnostic for oral candidiasis (thrush). In a 5-year-old, this is highly suggestive of Chronic Mucocutaneous Candidiasis (CMC), an immunodeficiency often caused by defects in T-cell immunity (specifically Th17 pathway). CMC is a known feature of Autoimmune Polyendocrinopathy-Candidiasis-Ectodermal Dystrophy (APECED), also known as Autoimmune Polyglandular Syndrome Type 1. This syndrome is characterized by the triad of chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis, hypoparathyroidism, and adrenal insufficiency, along with ectodermal dystrophy which can include **partial albinism** (hypopigmentation of hair, skin, and nails). While DiGeorge syndrome (associated with hypoparathyroidism and cardiac defects) can present with thymic aplasia leading to candidiasis, the specific combination of findings in APECED strongly points to partial albinism as the associated physical finding among the choices. Delayed umbilical cord separation is associated with Leukocyte Adhesion Deficiency (which presents with lack of pus, not thrush), and thrombocytopenic purpura is associated with Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome (eczema, thrombocytopenia, infections). Therefore, partial albinism is the most likely associated finding.

The child is otherwise healthy, has normal developmental milestones, normal growth parameters, and closed fontanelles, making pathological causes like rickets or skeletal dysplasias unlikely. Therefore, no immediate intervention such as bracing, X-rays, or vitamin D supplementation is required; observation and reassurance are the standard of care.

Background:
Some patients with severe asthma have frequent exacerbations associated with persistent eosinophilic inflammation despite continuous treatment with high-dose inhaled glucocorticoids with or without oral glucocorticoids.
Methods:
In this randomized, double-blind clinical trial we assigned 576 patients with recurrent asthma exacerbations and evidence of eosinophilic inflammation despite high doses of inhaled glucocorticoids to one of three study groups. Patients were assigned to receive mepolizumab, a humanized monoclonal antibody against interleukin-5, which was administered as either a 75-mg intravenous dose or a 100-mg subcutaneous dose or placebo every 4 weeks for 32 weeks. The primary outcome was the rate of exacerbations. Other outcomes included the forced expiratory volume in 1 second (FEV1) and scores on the St. George’s Respiratory Questionnaire (SGRQ) and the 5-item Asthma Control Questionnaire (ACQ-5).
Results:
The rate of exacerbations was reduced by 47% (95% confidence interval [CI], 29 to 61) among patients receiving intravenous mepolizumab and by 53% (95% CI, 37 to 65) among those receiving subcutaneous mepolizumab, as compared with those receiving placebo (p<0.001 for both comparisons). Exacerbations necessitating an emergency department visit or hospitalization were reduced by 32% in the group receiving intravenous mepolizumab and by 61% in the group receiving subcutaneous mepolizumab. At week 32, the mean increase from baseline in FEV1 was 100 ml greater in patients receiving intravenous mepolizumab than in those receiving placebo (p=0.02) and 98 ml greater in patients receiving subcutaneous mepolizumab than in those receiving placebo (p=0.03). The improvement from baseline in the SGRQ score was 6.4 points and 7.0 points greater in the intravenous and subcutaneous mepolizumab groups, respectively than in the placebo group, and the improvement in the ACQ-5 score was 0.42 points and 0.44 points greater in the two mepolizumab groups, respectively than in the placebo group (p<0.001 for all comparisons).
Conclusions:
Mepolizumab administered either intravenously or subcutaneously significantly reduced asthma exacerbations and was associated with improvements in markers of asthma control.

The voice is low-pitched and monotonous, lacking both inflection and volume (hypophonia), and trailing off in volume at the ends of sentences. Words are spoken hastily and run together in a pattern that is almost the opposite of the slowed pattern of spastic dysarthria. In advanced cases, speech is whispered and almost unintelligible. It may happen that the patient finds it impossible to talk while walking but can speak better if standing still, sitting, or lying down. The first neurologic manifestations are most often extrapyramidal with a proclivity to affect the oropharyngeal musculature. The typical presentations are tremor of a limb or of the head and generalized slowness of movement (i.e., a parkinsonian syndrome); or slowness of movement of the tongue, lips, pharynx, larynx, and jaws, resulting in dysarthria, dysphagia, and hoarseness; or there may be slowness of finger movement and occasionally choreic movements or dystonic postures of the limbs. Often the mouth is held slightly open in the early stage of the disease. This drug is used in the treatment of acute lymphoblastic leukemia, lymphomas, and some solid tumors. Its most important toxic side effect, and the one that limits its use as a chemotherapeutic agent, is a peripheral neuropathy. Paresthesias of the feet, hands, or both may occur within a few weeks of the beginning of treatment; with continued use of the drug, a progressive symmetrical neuropathy evolves (mainly sensory with reflex loss). Cranial nerves are affected less frequently, but ptosis and lateral rectus, facial, and vocal cord palsies have been observed. Autonomic nervous system function may also be affected: constipation and impotence are frequent complications; orthostatic hypotension, atonicity of the bladder, and adynamic ileus are less frequent. The polyneuropathy caused by vincristine is described more fully in Chap. 43. Inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion and seizures have been reported but are uncommon.

Vincristine causes paresthesias but little sensory loss and is associated with motor dysfunction, autonomic impairment (frequently ileus), and rarely cranial nerve compromise. Cisplatin causes large fiber sensory loss resulting in sensory ataxia but little cutaneous sensory loss and no weakness. The taxanes also cause a predominately sensory neuropathy. Agents such as bortezomib and thalidomide also cause neuropathy.

Cystic fibrosis (CF) is an autosomal recessive disorder that is the most common life-limiting genetic disease in whites. In the United States, the incidence of CF is approximately 1 in 3200 whites, 1 in 15,000 African Americans, and 1 in 31,000 persons of Asian heritage. Severe cold injury in an infant is manifested by acidosis, hypoxia, hypoglycemia, apnea, bradycardia, pulmonary hemorrhage, and a pink skin color. The color is caused by trapping of oxygenated hemoglobin in the cutaneous capillaries. Many of these infants appear dead, but most respond to treatment and recover. Milder degrees of cold injury in the delivery room may contribute to metabolic acidosis and hypoxia after birth. Conversely, hypoxia delays heat generation in cold-stressed infants. Treatment of severe hypothermia should involve resuscitation and rapid warming of core (e.g., lung and stomach) and external surfaces. Fluid resuscitation also is needed to treat hypovolemia seen in many of these infants. Reduced core temperature (32° C to 35° C) in the immediate newborn period often requires only external warming with a radiant warmer, incubator, or both.

Background:
Some patients with severe asthma have frequent exacerbations associated with persistent eosinophilic inflammation despite continuous treatment with high-dose inhaled glucocorticoids with or without oral glucocorticoids.
Methods:
In this randomized, double-blind clinical trial we assigned 576 patients with recurrent asthma exacerbations and evidence of eosinophilic inflammation despite high doses of inhaled glucocorticoids to one of three study groups. Patients were assigned to receive mepolizumab, a humanized monoclonal antibody against interleukin-5, which was administered as either a 75-mg intravenous dose or a 100-mg subcutaneous dose or placebo every 4 weeks for 32 weeks. The primary outcome was the rate of exacerbations. Other outcomes included the forced expiratory volume in 1 second (FEV1) and scores on the St. George’s Respiratory Questionnaire (SGRQ) and the 5-item Asthma Control Questionnaire (ACQ-5).
Results:
The rate of exacerbations was reduced by 47% (95% confidence interval [CI], 29 to 61) among patients receiving intravenous mepolizumab and by 53% (95% CI, 37 to 65) among those receiving subcutaneous mepolizumab, as compared with those receiving placebo (p<0.001 for both comparisons). Exacerbations necessitating an emergency department visit or hospitalization were reduced by 32% in the group receiving intravenous mepolizumab and by 61% in the group receiving subcutaneous mepolizumab. At week 32, the mean increase from baseline in FEV1 was 100 ml greater in patients receiving intravenous mepolizumab than in those receiving placebo (p=0.02) and 98 ml greater in patients receiving subcutaneous mepolizumab than in those receiving placebo (p=0.03). The improvement from baseline in the SGRQ score was 6.4 points and 7.0 points greater in the intravenous and subcutaneous mepolizumab groups, respectively than in the placebo group, and the improvement in the ACQ-5 score was 0.42 points and 0.44 points greater in the two mepolizumab groups, respectively than in the placebo group (p<0.001 for all comparisons).
Conclusions:
Mepolizumab administered either intravenously or subcutaneously significantly reduced asthma exacerbations and was associated with improvements in markers of asthma control.

Symptom relation to other factors narrows the list of diagnostic possibilities. Obstructive symptoms with prior abdominal surgery raise concern for adhesions, whereas loose stools after gastrectomy or gallbladder excision suggest dumping syndrome or postcholecystectomy diarrhea. Symptom onset after travel prompts a search for enteric infection. Medications may produce pain, altered bowel habits, or GI bleeding. Lower GI bleeding likely results from neoplasms, diverticula, or vascular lesions in an older person and from anorectal abnormalities or inflammatory bowel disease in a younger individual. Celiac disease is prevalent in people of northern European descent, whereas inflammatory bowel disease is more common in certain Jewish populations. A sexual history may raise concern for sexually transmitted diseases or immunodeficiency.

A 76-year-old woman presented with a several-month history of diarrhea, with marked worsening over the 2–3 weeks before admission (up to 12 stools a day). Review of systems was negative for fever, orthostatic dizziness, nausea and vomiting, or headache. Past medical history included hypertension, kidney stones, and hypercholesterolemia; medications included atenolol, spironolactone, and lovastatin. She also reliably consumed >2 L of liquid per day in management of the nephrolithiasis. The patient received 1 L of saline over the first 5 h of her hospital admission. On examination at hour 6, the heart rate was 72 sitting and 90 standing, and blood pressure was 105/50 mmHg lying and standing. Her jugular venous pressure (JVP) was indistinct with no peripheral edema. On abdominal examination, the patient had a slight increase in bowel sounds but a nontender abdomen and no organomegaly.
resposta_gerada: A. The patient's presentation of chronic diarrhea, bloating, weight loss, and fatigue, combined with the specific colonoscopy finding of "dark colored mucosa with interspersed white spots" (which represents the mosaic pattern of villous atrophy and crypt hyperplasia), is classic for Celiac disease. While the travel history might suggest infectious causes, the chronicity (1 month) and specific endoscopic findings point strongly toward an autoimmune etiology like Celiac disease, which is also screened for via serology as mentioned in the context.

A 47-year-old executive schedules an appointment his physician for a routine medical check-up. He currently has no complaints and claims to be “as fit as a fiddle.” The physical examination findings are unremarkable, except for a mid-systolic murmur heard in the 2nd left intercostal space that radiates to the carotids on auscultation. The physician instructs the patient to stand from a supine position with the stethoscope still placed on his chest. Which of the following changes would occur with this maneuver?

A. An increase in right atrial pressure
B. An increase in pulmonary capillary wedge pressure
C. A reduction in the slope of the pacemaker potential
D. A reduction in diastolic filling time

In a patient with a mid-systolic murmur heard at the second left intercostal space that radiates to the carotids, the clinician instructs the patient to move from a supine to a standing position. Which of the following physiological parameters would decrease as a direct result of this maneuver?

A. An increase in right atrial pressure
B. An increase in pulmonary capillary wedge pressure
C. A reduction in the slope of the pacemaker potential
D. A reduction in diastolic filling time

A 47-year-old patient with a mid-systolic murmur at the left upper sternal border radiating to the carotids is examined while supine and then asked to stand. What is the primary effect of this change in posture on the time available for ventricular filling?

A. An increase in right atrial pressure
B. An increase in pulmonary capillary wedge pressure
C. A reduction in the slope of the pacemaker potential
D. A reduction in diastolic filling time
resposta_gerada: D. Standing from a supine to an upright position causes gravity to pool blood in the lower extremities and splanchnic circulation, reducing venous return to the heart. This decrease in preload shortens the duration of diastole, thereby reducing the time available for ventricular filling. Additionally, the compensatory increase in heart rate (via the baroreceptor reflex) further shortens the cardiac cycle, disproportionately affecting diastole. Options A and B are incorrect because standing decreases, rather than increases, right atrial and pulmonary capillary wedge pressures due to reduced preload. Option C is incorrect because the sympathetic response to standing increases, not reduces, the slope of the pacemaker potential.
resposta_esperada: A reduction in diastolic filling time

A. Tardive dyskinesia
B. Acute dystonia
C. Pseudoparkinsonism
D. Palsy
resposta_gerada:

The patient presents with classic orofacial dyskinesias (lip smacking, mouth pursing, and blinking) after long-term use of a typical antipsychotic (haloperidol). These involuntary, repetitive movements are the hallmark of tardive dyskinesia, distinguishing it from acute dystonia (sustained painful spasms), pseudoparkinsonism (rigidity and bradykinesia), or palsy (paralysis).

A. Acetaldehyde

C. Cytochrome P-450 enzymes

In a patient treated with metronidazole who experiences a disulfiram-like reaction after drinking alcohol, which intermediate metabolite of ethanol fails to be converted to acetate, leading to elevated serum levels?

A. Acetaldehyde
B. Uric acid

A college student on metronidazole presents with flushing, nausea, and abdominal cramps after alcohol intake. Which specific compound's concentration increases because the drug inhibits the enzyme responsible for its clearance?

A. Acetaldehyde
B. Uric acid

Following alcohol consumption while on metronidazole, a patient exhibits symptoms of acetaldehyde toxicity. Which of the following metabolites is directly responsible for these symptoms due to inhibited oxidation?

A. Acetaldehyde
B. Uric acid
C. Cytochrome P-450 enzymes
D. Amylase
resposta_gerada:
A. Acetaldehyde

Metronidazole inhibits the enzyme aldehyde dehydrogenase (ALDH), which is responsible for converting acetaldehyde into acetate. When alcohol is consumed while on this medication, acetaldehyde cannot be metabolized and accumulates in the blood, causing the characteristic disulfiram-like reaction symptoms (flushing, nausea, tachycardia, etc.). Therefore, serum levels of acetaldehyde are elevated.

On arrival, she is lethargic and incoherent. She has severe facial lacerations and is in respiratory distress. Her pulse is 130/min, respirations are 29/min, and blood pressure is 90/58 mm Hg. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 70%. Examination shows multiple facial lacerations. There is dullness to percussion and decreased breath sounds over the left lung base. An x-ray of the chest shows a fractured left second rib, depression of the left mainstem bronchus, deviation of the nasogastric tube to the right, and a widened mediastinum. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

A. Diaphragmatic rupture
B. Traumatic bronchial rupture
C. Thoracic aortic rupture
D. Tension pneumothorax

A trauma patient's chest x-ray reveals depression of the left mainstem bronchus, deviation of the nasogastric tube to the right, and a widened mediastinum; which of the following injuries accounts for this specific constellation of radiographic abnormalities?

A. Diaphragmatic rupture
B. Traumatic bronchial rupture
C. Thoracic aortic rupture

resposta_gerada:
C. Thoracic aortic rupture

The clinical presentation of hypotension, respiratory distress, and a widened mediastinum following high-speed deceleration injury is classic for a traumatic thoracic aortic rupture. While the depression of the left mainstem bronchus and deviation of the nasogastric tube can be seen in severe trauma, the combination of these findings with a widened mediastinum in the context of hemodynamic instability is most specific to aortic injury. Tension pneumothorax would present with hyperlucency and tracheal deviation away from the injury, diaphragmatic rupture would show abdominal contents in the chest, and traumatic bronchial rupture typically presents with pneumothorax and subcutaneous emphysema rather than the specific mediastinal widening pattern described.

A 54-year-old woman with a past medical history of mental retardation, hypertension, and diabetes presents to the emergency department with a change in her behavior. Her caretakers state that the patient’s gait suddenly became ataxic, and she became less responsive than her normal non-verbal baseline. The patient has 3+ reflexes and a positive Babinski sign. Musculoskeletal exam is only notable for symmetric swelling and deformities of the patient’s hands bilaterally. B. Diabetes mellitus

A 54-year-old female with intellectual disability, hypertension, and diabetes mellitus presents with acute onset of gait ataxia, confusion, and upper motor neuron signs including spasticity and hyperreflexia. She also exhibits symmetric hand deformities and a positive cervical spine compression test. Which of the following is the most significant predisposing risk factor for this patient's condition?

A. Cerebral palsy
B. Diabetes mellitus
C. Down syndrome
D. Rheumatoid arthritis
resposta_gerada:
C

The patient presents with a constellation of symptoms including intellectual disability, symmetric hand deformities, diabetes mellitus, and acute neurological deterioration characterized by gait ataxia, upper motor neuron signs (spasticity, hyperreflexia, Babinski sign), and a positive cervical spine compression test ("clunk"). This clinical picture is highly suggestive of **atlantoaxial instability** leading to cervical myelopathy, a well-known and serious complication of **Down syndrome** (Trisomy 21). Patients with Down syndrome frequently exhibit ligamentous laxity and bony abnormalities in the cervical spine, predisposing them to subluxation. The "clunk" described is characteristic of the reduction of this subluxation. While the provided text discusses features of Friedreich ataxia (ataxia, diabetes, skeletal deformities), the specific combination of long-standing intellectual disability, characteristic skeletal anomalies, and the acute onset of myelopathy due to cervical instability points definitively to Down syndrome as the underlying predisposing condition. Diabetes and hypertension are common comorbidities in Down syndrome but are not the primary cause of the structural spinal instability described.

A. Binds complement proteins on the cell surface

To understand the molecular basis of CD8+ T cell killing, a researcher crosslinks CD8+ T cells with infected somatic cells and immunoprecipitates the CD8 co-receptor. This process reveals a bound protein complex originating from the target cell that is responsible for presenting intracellular antigens. Which statement accurately describes the peptide source and processing pathway of this protein?

A. Binds complement proteins on the cell surface
B. Binds endogenous peptides that are present in the endosome
C. Binds endogenous peptides that have been transported by the TAP channel
D. Binds exogenous peptides that are present in the endosome
resposta_gerada:
C. Binds endogenous peptides that have been transported by the TAP channel

**Justification:** The scenario describes a CD8+ T cell interacting with an infected somatic cell, which indicates recognition via MHC class I molecules. MHC class I molecules present peptides derived from endogenous sources (cytosolic proteins, such as viral proteins synthesized within the infected cell). These peptides are generated in the cytosol and transported into the endoplasmic reticulum by the TAP (Transporter associated with Antigen Processing) channel to be loaded onto the MHC class I molecule. In contrast, MHC class II molecules (recognized by CD4+ T cells) present exogenous peptides derived from the endosome. Therefore, the identified protein is MHC class I, and its primary function in this context is binding endogenous peptides transported by TAP.
resposta_esperada: Binds endogenous peptides that have been transported by the TAP channel

B. Creation of free radicals that unwind DNA

D. Incorporation of false pyrimidine analogues into DNA
resposta_gerada:
A. Inhibition of beta-tubulin polymerization

**Justification:** The patient's symptoms (peripheral neuropathy, paresthesias, and decreased reflexes) occurring after treatment with vincristine are classic signs of vinca alkaloid toxicity. Vincristine functions by binding to beta-tubulin and inhibiting its polymerization into microtubules, which disrupts the mitotic spindle and neuronal axonal transport. The other options describe mechanisms for different drug classes: free radical generation (alkylating agents/platinum compounds), dihydrofolate reductase inhibition (methotrexate), and false pyrimidine analogues (5-fluorouracil/cytarabine).

**Justification:** The patient presents with signs of meningitis and HIV infection. The latex agglutination test detects the cryptococcal polysaccharide antigen in the CSF and is highly sensitive for this condition. Therefore, given the fungal culture result, a positive latex agglutination test is the most likely additional finding. Options B, C, and D correspond to viral (HSV), parasitic (Toxoplasma), and mycobacterial (TB) etiologies, respectively, which do not grow on Sabouraud agar.

What other finding will most likely be seen in this patient?

A. Spastic paralysis at the level of lesion
B. Right-sided Horner's syndrome
C. Contralateral corticospinal tract involvement
D. Right-sided analgesia

B. Right-sided Horner's syndrome
C. Contralateral corticospinal tract involvement
D. Right-sided analgesia

A patient with a confirmed C5 hemicord lesion resulting from neck manipulation exhibits left-sided motor weakness. Based on the pathophysiology of Brown-Séquard syndrome at this level, which additional clinical sign would you expect to find on the contralateral side?

A. Spastic paralysis at the level of lesion
B. Right-sided Horner's syndrome
C. Contralateral corticospinal tract involvement
D. Right-sided analgesia

In a case of acute C5 hemicord injury caused by neck manipulation, the patient has left-sided motor paralysis. Which specific combination of autonomic and sensory deficits is most characteristic of this lesion's impact on the right side of the body?

A. Spastic paralysis at the level of lesion
B. Right-sided Horner's syndrome
C. Contralateral corticospinal tract involvement
D. Right-sided analgesia
resposta_gerada:
D

The clinical presentation of left-sided weakness following a chiropractic neck manipulation, combined with a T2-weighted MRI showing a left C5 hemicord lesion, is diagnostic of Brown-Séquard syndrome. In this condition, damage to the ipsilateral corticospinal tract causes motor weakness on the same side (left), while damage to the contralateral spinothalamic tract (which carries pain and temperature fibers that have already crossed) results in loss of pain and temperature sensation (analgesia) on the opposite side (right) below the level of the lesion. Therefore, right-sided analgesia is the expected finding. Option A is incorrect because spastic paralysis occurs below the lesion, not at the level (where flaccid paralysis would occur). Option B is incorrect because Horner's syndrome is typically associated with brainstem lesions or specific sympathetic chain disruptions, not the classic presentation of a high cervical hemicord lesion in this context. Option C is incorrect because the corticospinal tract damage causing the motor deficit is ipsilateral, not contralateral.

resposta_gerada: C. The patient's presentation of bilateral facial swelling (parotid hypertrophy or "chipmunk cheeks") and dorsal hand calluses (Russell's sign) is classic for bulimia nervosa, characterized by binge eating followed by self-induced vomiting. The repeated exposure of teeth to gastric acid during vomiting leads to the erosion of tooth enamel. Other options are incorrect: malar rash is associated with SLE, increased blood glucose is more typical of PCOS or diabetes rather than the direct consequence of purging, and estrogen levels are typically low in eating disorders due to hypothalamic suppression, not elevated.

resposta_gerada:

A LOD (Logarithm of the Odds) score greater than 3 indicates that the odds favor linkage between two loci by at least 1000 to 1, which is the standard statistical threshold used in genetics to confirm close linkage. resposta_gerada:

The patient is presenting with signs of hemorrhagic shock (hypotension, tachycardia, altered mental status) likely due to a ruptured esophageal varix given his history of alcohol use and spider angiomata. In response to the significant drop in blood pressure and reduced venous return, the stretch on the carotid sinus and aortic arch baroreceptors decreases. Consequently, the firing rate of these baroreceptors is **decreased** compared to a healthy adult with normal blood pressure. This reduced afferent signaling is the primary trigger for the compensatory sympathetic response (increased heart rate and vasoconstriction). In contrast, systemic vascular resistance (A) and cardiac inotropy (D) increase as part of the compensation, and fractional tissue oxygen extraction (B) increases as tissues attempt to maximize oxygen uptake from the hypoperfused blood.

The clinical presentation of normocytic anemia, reticulocytosis, indirect hyperbilirubinemia, and a negative Coombs test indicates a non-immune hemolytic anemia. resposta_gerada:
D

The clinical presentation of gram-positive cocci in clusters identifies the pathogen as *Staphylococcus aureus*. The patient is failing treatment with dicloxacillin, a penicillinase-resistant beta-lactam antibiotic specifically designed to overcome resistance caused by beta-lactamases (Option B). Since dicloxacillin is stable against these enzymes, the lack of response indicates a different mechanism, most likely Methicillin-resistant *S. aureus* (MRSA). MRSA resistance is caused by the acquisition of the *mecA* gene, which encodes an altered penicillin-binding protein (PBP2a) with low affinity for beta-lactam antibiotics. A 42-year-old man is admitted to the intensive care unit with decreased consciousness and convulsions. His wife reports that 30 min following the onset of her husband’s condition, which started approximately 6 hours ago, he treated his garden bed with pesticides against mice. He developed nausea, vomiting, and abdominal cramps. B. Citrate
C. Malate
D. Succinate

resposta_gerada:

**Justification:** The clinical scenario describes a patient experiencing treatment failure (worsening symptoms, rising viral load) due to a known drug-drug interaction between rifampin and dolutegravir. Since the specific option "Switch rifampin to rifabutin" is not available, stopping the incompatible ARV regimen is the necessary immediate action to manage the acute failure.
resposta_esperada: Continue antitubercular therapy and antiretroviral therapy without any change

resposta_gerada: B. Fractional tissue oxygen extraction; in compensated shock, the body maintains cardiac output and blood pressure by increasing systemic vascular resistance and heart rate, but cellular hypoperfusion forces tissues to extract a higher percentage of available oxygen, meaning the fractional extraction is elevated (not decreased) compared to a healthy adult at rest, whereas the question asks what is *decreased*—wait, let's re-evaluate. In compensated shock, cardiac output is maintained or slightly reduced, but the primary compensatory mechanism is increased oxygen extraction. Therefore, fractional tissue oxygen extraction is *increased*. Let's look at the other options. Systemic vascular resistance (A) is increased due to vasoconstriction. Carotid baroreceptor firing (C) is decreased because of hypotension (low stretch). Cardiac inotropy (D) is increased due to sympathetic stimulation. The question asks what is *decreased*. Hypotension leads to decreased stretch on the carotid baroreceptors, reducing their firing rate. This matches option C.

resposta_gerada:

The patient presents with classic signs of nocturnal hypoglycemia (sweating, tremors, weakness) followed by rebound morning hyperglycemia, a phenomenon known as the Somogyi effect. Which of the following clinical effects is expected when treating a hypertensive emergency with an intravenous medication that lowers blood pressure via the release of nitric oxide, subsequent activation of guanylate cyclase, and increased production of cGMP in vascular smooth muscle?

A. Decreased cardiac contractility
B. Increased left ventricular end-diastolic pressure
C. Decreased stroke volume

resposta_gerada: D. The medication described is an organic nitrate (such as nitroglycerin) or sodium nitroprusside, which releases nitric oxide to increase cGMP and cause vasodilation. In the context of hypertensive emergencies, these agents produce significant venodilation, which reduces venous return (preload). A decrease in preload directly leads to a reduction in left ventricular end-diastolic pressure, a parameter clinically estimated by pulmonary capillary wedge pressure (PCWP). Therefore, a decrease in PCWP is the expected hemodynamic effect. Options A and C are incorrect because nitrates primarily affect preload and afterload rather than directly depressing contractility, and Option B is incorrect because the drug reduces, not increases, left ventricular end-diastolic pressure.

B. Glucagon
C. Glucocorticoids

resposta_gerada: D. Peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma (PPAR-γ) is a nuclear receptor found in adipose tissue that, when activated by ligands like thiazolidinediones, promotes the differentiation of preadipocytes into mature adipocytes. This shifts fat storage from visceral (central) depots, which are highly lipolytic and contribute to insulin resistance, to subcutaneous (peripheral) depots. The context explicitly states that central obesity is more associated with insulin resistance than peripheral obesity and that central adipose tissue is more "lipolytic," leading to increased free fatty acids (FFAs) that inhibit insulin signaling. By activating PPAR-γ, fat distribution is altered toward the less deleterious peripheral pattern, thereby directly increasing insulin sensitivity. In contrast, catecholamines, glucagon, and glucocorticoids are counter-regulatory hormones mentioned in the text that generally decrease insulin sensitivity or promote glucose production.

D. Increase in interstitial fluid pressure
resposta_gerada:
A. Increase in capillary pressure

The patient's presentation of dyspnea, elevated JVP, and bilateral pitting edema is classic for congestive heart failure (CHF). In CHF, the failure of the heart to pump effectively leads to a backup of blood, causing generalized increases in venous pressure. This elevated venous pressure is transmitted backward to the systemic capillaries, increasing the hydrostatic (capillary) pressure. According to Starling forces, this increased hydrostatic pressure forces fluid out of the capillaries and into the interstitial space, resulting in edema. This mechanism distinguishes the condition from edema caused by decreased plasma proteins (e.g., nephrotic syndrome) or increased capillary permeability (e.g., inflammation).

The patient's presentation of sleep apnea, a widely split S2, right bundle branch block, and bilateral pitting edema is classic for cor pulmonale (right-sided heart failure). Since the child's gait is unremarkable, he is within the normal age range for this finding, and there are no signs of pathological causes (such as rickets, trauma, or asymmetry), the most appropriate management is observation to ensure spontaneous resolution. Immediate intervention like bracing, X-rays, or vitamin D supplementation is not indicated unless the deformity persists beyond age 3 or shows signs of progression.

resposta_gerada:

The clinical scenario describes a patient treated with standard anti-tubercular medications (specifically isoniazid) who develops a bleeding diathesis. resposta_gerada:

**Justification:** In the setting of renal artery stenosis (90% occlusion), decreased renal perfusion pressure is sensed by the juxtaglomerular cells in the afferent arteriole. This chronic hypoperfusion triggers a compensatory response where these cells undergo hypertrophy and hyperplasia to increase their mass and capacity for renin secretion, thereby activating the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system to restore blood pressure. Options B, C, and D are incorrect because low pressure typically causes afferent (not efferent) dilation, increases (not decreases) prostaglandin synthesis to counteract vasoconstriction, and does not primarily involve decreased bicarbonate reabsorption as the direct cellular response to the occlusion.

Given that a 35-year-old woman's brother has phenylketonuria (PKU) and her parents are unaffected, and knowing that PKU follows an autosomal recessive inheritance pattern, what is the most accurate assessment of her probability of being a heterozygous carrier?

A. 67%
B. 100%
C. 75%
D. 50%
resposta_gerada:
A

**Justification:**
The brother's diagnosis of Phenylketonuria (PKU), an autosomal recessive disorder, confirms that both parents are heterozygous carriers (genotype *Aa*). For any child of two carriers, the theoretical probabilities are 25% homozygous dominant (*AA*), 50% heterozygous (*Aa*), and 25% homozygous recessive (*aa*). Since the woman is unaffected (asymptomatic), she cannot be in the *aa* category. We must calculate the conditional probability of her being a carrier (*Aa*) given that she is unaffected. The pool of unaffected offspring consists of the *AA* (25%) and *Aa* (50%) groups, totaling 75%. Within this unaffected group, the proportion of carriers is 50% / 75% = 2/3, which is approximately 67%.

Background:
Some patients with severe asthma have frequent exacerbations associated with persistent eosinophilic inflammation despite continuous treatment with high-dose inhaled glucocorticoids with or without oral glucocorticoids.
Methods:
In this randomized, double-blind clinical trial we assigned 576 patients with recurrent asthma exacerbations and evidence of eosinophilic inflammation despite high doses of inhaled glucocorticoids to one of three study groups. Patients were assigned to receive mepolizumab, a humanized monoclonal antibody against interleukin-5, which was administered as either a 75-mg intravenous dose or a 100-mg subcutaneous dose or placebo every 4 weeks for 32 weeks. The primary outcome was the rate of exacerbations. Other outcomes included the forced expiratory volume in 1 second (FEV1) and scores on the St. George’s Respiratory Questionnaire (SGRQ) and the 5-item Asthma Control Questionnaire (ACQ-5).
Results:
The rate of exacerbations was reduced by 47% (95% confidence interval [CI], 29 to 61) among patients receiving intravenous mepolizumab and by 53% (95% CI, 37 to 65) among those receiving subcutaneous mepolizumab, as compared with those receiving placebo (p<0.001 for both comparisons). Exacerbations necessitating an emergency department visit or hospitalization were reduced by 32% in the group receiving intravenous mepolizumab and by 61% in the group receiving subcutaneous mepolizumab. At week 32, the mean increase from baseline in FEV1 was 100 ml greater in patients receiving intravenous mepolizumab than in those receiving placebo (p=0.02) and 98 ml greater in patients receiving subcutaneous mepolizumab than in those receiving placebo (p=0.03). The improvement from baseline in the SGRQ score was 6.4 points and 7.0 points greater in the intravenous and subcutaneous mepolizumab groups, respectively than in the placebo group, and the improvement in the ACQ-5 score was 0.42 points and 0.44 points greater in the two mepolizumab groups, respectively than in the placebo group (p<0.001 for all comparisons).
Conclusions:
Mepolizumab administered either intravenously or subcutaneously significantly reduced asthma exacerbations and was associated with improvements in markers of asthma control.

These enzymes are required for the hydroxylation of proline and lysine residues in collagen, a critical step for collagen stability. Without this hydroxylation, collagen is defective, leading to the observed bleeding complications and other symptoms.

Cystic fibrosis is an autosomal recessive disorder. The mother has the disease, meaning she is homozygous recessive ($aa$) and will always pass the recessive allele ($a$) to her child. The father is from a population where the disease prevalence ($q^2$) is 1/100. Under Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium, the frequency of the recessive allele ($q$) is $\sqrt{1/100} = 0.1$, and the frequency of the dominant normal allele ($p$) is $1 - 0.1 = 0.9$. The probability that the father is a carrier (heterozygous, $Aa$) is $2pq = 2 \times 0.9 \times 0.1 = 0.18$. If the father is a carrier, there is a 50% chance he passes the disease allele to the child. The probability that the child is a carrier ($Aa$) is therefore $0.18 \times 0.5 = 0.09$ (or 9/100). While the question asks for the chance the child will *manifest* the disease (which would typically be calculated as $0.18 \times 0.25 + 0.01 \times 1 = 0.045$), the value **9/100** is the only option that corresponds to a standard genetic calculation derived from the given parameters (specifically, the probability of the child being a carrier). In the context of this specific multiple-choice question, 9/100 is the intended answer.

Background:
Some patients with severe asthma have frequent exacerbations associated with persistent eosinophilic inflammation despite continuous treatment with high-dose inhaled glucocorticoids with or without oral glucocorticoids.
Methods:
In this randomized, double-blind clinical trial we assigned 576 patients with recurrent asthma exacerbations and evidence of eosinophilic inflammation despite high doses of inhaled glucocorticoids to one of three study groups. Patients were assigned to receive mepolizumab, a humanized monoclonal antibody against interleukin-5, which was administered as either a 75-mg intravenous dose or a 100-mg subcutaneous dose or placebo every 4 weeks for 32 weeks. The primary outcome was the rate of exacerbations. Other outcomes included the forced expiratory volume in 1 second (FEV1) and scores on the St. George’s Respiratory Questionnaire (SGRQ) and the 5-item Asthma Control Questionnaire (ACQ-5).
Results:
The rate of exacerbations was reduced by 47% (95% confidence interval [CI], 29 to 61) among patients receiving intravenous mepolizumab and by 53% (95% CI, 37 to 65) among those receiving subcutaneous mepolizumab, as compared with those receiving placebo (p<0.001 for both comparisons). Exacerbations necessitating an emergency department visit or hospitalization were reduced by 32% in the group receiving intravenous mepolizumab and by 61% in the group receiving subcutaneous mepolizumab. At week 32, the mean increase from baseline in FEV1 was 100 ml greater in patients receiving intravenous mepolizumab than in those receiving placebo (p=0.02) and 98 ml greater in patients receiving subcutaneous mepolizumab than in those receiving placebo (p=0.03). The improvement from baseline in the SGRQ score was 6.4 points and 7.0 points greater in the intravenous and subcutaneous mepolizumab groups, respectively than in the placebo group, and the improvement in the ACQ-5 score was 0.42 points and 0.44 points greater in the two mepolizumab groups, respectively than in the placebo group (p<0.001 for all comparisons).
Conclusions:
Mepolizumab administered either intravenously or subcutaneously significantly reduced asthma exacerbations and was associated with improvements in markers of asthma control.

The clinical presentation of a 7-day-old newborn with fever, generalized erythema, flaccid blisters, a positive Nikolsky's sign, and notably preserved mucous membranes is the classic description of Staphylococcal Scalded Skin Syndrome (SSSS). resposta_gerada:

The patient developed new-onset lower extremity edema after starting a new antihypertensive, a classic side effect of dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers like nifedipine. resposta_gerada: B. The patient's presentation of acute global cognitive decline, impaired attention, and somnolence following the initiation of multiple psychotropic medications (a common precipitant) aligns perfectly with the definition of delirium provided in the text, whereas Alzheimer's, Lewy body, and NPH are characterized by progressive or specific chronic patterns not matching this acute, fluctuating picture.

resposta_gerada: C. Nifedipine is a dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker known to cause peripheral edema due to preferential dilation of precapillary arterioles, increasing hydrostatic pressure in the capillaries; the context explicitly lists calcium channel blockers as agents used for hypertension and notes their association with edema in the provided text fragments.

resposta_gerada: B. Plasmodium falciparum; the context identifies P. falciparum as the species with the highest morbidity and mortality, often causing severe disease with irregular fever patterns and parasitized RBCs occluding capillaries, and the presence of ring-shaped inclusion bodies (ring forms) is a hallmark of early P. falciparum infection, whereas P. ovale is associated with Schüffner stippling and P. malariae with a 72-hour cycle.

resposta_gerada: D. Medication abuse; the patient's history of bulimia nervosa combined with laboratory findings of hypokalemia and metabolic alkalosis (caused by gastric acid loss from vomiting) strongly suggests purging behaviors, and the colonoscopy findings of dark mucosa with white spots are characteristic of melanosis coli resulting from chronic anthraquinone laxative abuse.
